pages.title: Canvas2D stays the default terminal renderer; the GPU path ships opt-in because we cannot blocklist bad drivers
pages.body:
## What we measured

On a flood test (`yes | head -c 50M`, 200x50 grid) xterm-addon-webgl 0.16 held 58 fps where the canvas2d addon held 22, and cut main-thread time per frame from 41 ms to 9 ms. Nobody disputes the numbers; the decision is not about speed.

## Why it is still off

Between 2024-11 and 2025-02 we collected 37 crash reports where the whole webview process died inside the GPU command buffer. Every one was an Intel integrated GPU: HD 4000 / UHD 620 on Windows, and the 2015-era dual-GPU MacBook Pros. A dead webview takes every pane with it, including agent panes mid-run, so a rendering optimisation was costing people unrecoverable work.

The obvious mitigation — ship our own driver blocklist — does not work in our shell. Tauri renders in WKWebView on macOS and WebView2 on Windows. `WEBGL_debug_renderer_info` was removed in Safari 17 and is gated behind a flag in recent Chromium, so the strings we get back are `Apple GPU` and `Google Inc.` and nothing else. We cannot identify the driver we would need to exclude, and Chromium's own blocklist is not queryable from page context.

## Shape of the decision

Default is canvas2d. `terminal.renderer = "webgl"` turns the GPU path on with a one-time banner saying it may take the window down. Revisit when either the addon stops doing raw per-frame texture uploads or the webview exposes the adapter.

pages.title: WebGL is now the default renderer and canvas survives only as a per-pane crash fallback
pages.body:
## What changed since the opt-in decision

Four things, all of them external to the choice itself:

1. xterm 5.5 with addon 0.18 rewrote the glyph cache to shelf packing and stopped re-uploading whole textures per frame, which is where the command-buffer crashes were concentrated (see [[render-atlas-eviction-thrash]]).
2. We landed per-pane recovery for a lost drawing context ([[render-context-loss-after-sleep]]). A failure now demotes one pane instead of killing the webview, so the worst case went from "lose the workspace" to "this pane gets slower".
3. Telemetry from the 2.4.x beta channel, where the GPU path was forced on: 0 GPU-process crashes across 11 400 sessions, 61 context losses, all recovered.
4. Tauri 2.1 pins WebView2 evergreen >= 122 and raises the macOS floor to 12.0. That drops the entire HD 4000 fleet — 0.4% of installs, and they land on canvas anyway.

## The rule now

`auto` means WebGL. A pane falls back to canvas permanently when init fails or after three context losses inside 60 seconds, and the reason is written to the renderer log. `dom` remains only for accessibility snapshot tests. The explicit setting stays because support needs it for reproductions, not because we expect users to touch it.

One regression we accepted: the first frame of a new pane is ~18 ms slower on the GPU path because the glyph cache starts cold.

pages.title: Programming ligatures are on out of the box, shaped in JS rather than pre-shaped in the Rust core
pages.body:
## Why on by default

Three of the five fonts we bundle (JetBrains Mono, Fira Code, Cascadia Code) carry `calt` rules, and iTerm2, WezTerm and Kitty all render them without being asked. In the beta survey, 71 of 94 respondents said a terminal that draws `=>` as two characters looks broken to them. Shipping the feature behind a checkbox meant most users would never see the fonts we paid attention to.

## Why the shaping happens in the webview

We prototyped shaping in the Rust core with rustybuzz and sending pre-shaped runs across the Tauri bridge. It was rejected: the renderer needs shaping results for the visible viewport and re-asks on every scroll tick, so the bridge call sits inside the frame path. Measured round-trip through the Tauri IPC was 0.8-2.0 ms per call even with the payload cached, which is a quarter of a frame budget before any drawing happens. Making it async instead means a frame drawn with last frame's shaping — visible tearing of the glyph run during fast scroll.

So we use xterm-addon-ligatures 0.9, which hooks `registerCharacterJoiner`, does the shaping with the `font-ligatures` package in JS, and caches per (font, string). Both the canvas and the GPU renderer honour joiners, so the choice does not pin us to one renderer.

## Known rough edge

The joiner works on plain text of a row, so a row containing an SGR change in the middle of what would be a ligature does not join. That matches other terminals and we are not fixing it.

pages.title: Ligatures are off by default: shaping cost 6-9 ms a frame and made per-cell drawing lie about positions
pages.body:
## The cost

Profiling an agent pane streaming a unified diff at 200x50: the character joiner ran for every changed row of every frame. `font-ligatures` keys its cache on the whole row string, so a line being appended to in place misses the cache on every single write. Median 6.1 ms per frame on an M1, 9.4 ms on a Windows laptop with the same content — on top of the 4-6 ms the draw itself costs. On fast output the pane fell to roughly 30 fps with the feature on and stayed at 60 with it off.

## The part that was actually a bug

A joined run is drawn as a single wide glyph, so everything that assumes one cell equals one drawn unit becomes wrong:

- Selecting half of `!==` highlights the whole run.
- A block caret parked on the `=` of `=>` paints over both cells.
- Search highlighting (the decoration API) drifts right by one cell for every joined run earlier in the row.

Users filed all of this as "the text insertion point is in the wrong place after I scroll", which is why it took two releases before anyone connected it to font shaping at all.

## Now

`terminal.ligatures` defaults to false. Panes owned by the agent orchestrator force it off regardless of the setting, because that is where both the throughput and the selection problems bite hardest. The `calt` fonts stay bundled.

pages.title: The glyph texture collapses to 8 fps past ~1400 distinct characters because a full atlas was cleared wholesale
pages.body:
## Symptom

Tailing a build log with Chinese log messages, or `less`-ing a file of mixed CJK, drops the pane to 6-9 fps with the GPU at 100%. Latin-only output of the same volume runs at 60. Reproduces with a loop printing 4 000 distinct CJK codepoints into a 200x50 pane.

## Cause

The GPU renderer rasterises each glyph once into a single 2048x2048 texture, packed into fixed 16-row shelves. When the last shelf filled, addon 0.16 called `clearAtlas()` — the whole texture, every glyph, gone — and re-rasterised on demand. Once the working set of a screen plus its scrollback redraw exceeded what the shelves hold (about 1400 double-width glyphs, fewer than the naive area calculation suggests because shelf height is fixed and CJK is tall), every frame overflowed again: clear, re-rasterise ~1400 glyphs at roughly 0.05 ms each through the 2D context, overflow, clear. The steady state is 70+ ms of rasterisation per frame and no forward progress.

## Fix and rejected fix

A second texture page plus LRU eviction of individual shelves, so overflow costs one shelf and not the world. Cap is 2 pages; a third overflow inside one second demotes the pane to canvas for the rest of its life.

Simply raising the texture to 4096x4096 was rejected: `MAX_TEXTURE_SIZE` is 4096 on several Intel drivers we still support, so there would have been no headroom left for a second page, and a cold upload of a 4096² atlas costs over 30 ms on those same drivers.

pages.title: Смена темы не перекрашивала уже выведенный текст: ключ кэша глифа хранил индекс палитры, а не цвет
pages.body:
## Симптом

Переключение Light → Dark: в панелях, которые уже что-то вывели, старые строки остаются нарисованными прежним цветом — тёмное на тёмном, читать невозможно. Новые строки рисуются правильно. Прокрутка не помогает, помогает только пересоздание панели.

## Причина

Кэш растрированных глифов адресуется ключом (codepoint, bold, italic, dim, fgIndex). Для цветов из темы `fgIndex` — это номер слота 0..15, а не RGB. Переключение темы меняет отображение слот → RGB, но сам ключ остаётся прежним, поэтому кэш отдаёт растр, нарисованный старой краской.

Что сбивало с толку три недели: для 24-битных цветов (SGR 38;2) в ключ идёт сам RGB, и вывод `ls --color` или подсветка в `bat` перекрашивались корректно. Ломался только текст, использующий стандартные шестнадцать слотов — то есть в основном приглашение оболочки и вывод ошибок.

## Решение и отклонённый вариант

В ключ добавлен счётчик поколения темы; событие `theme:changed` инкрементирует его, вызывает сброс текстуры и полную перерисовку всех живых панелей (11-40 мс на панель, разово).

Отклонено: растрировать глиф белым и умножать на цвет в шейдере. Ломается субпиксельное сглаживание — растр зависит от цвета фона, а не только переднего плана — и не работает для цветных эмодзи, которые приходят из системного шрифта уже раскрашенными. Про то, как цвета темы вообще попадают в палитру, см. [[render-theme-palette-contrast]].

pages.title: Panes go black after wake because a lost GPU drawing context was never restored and draw calls silently no-op
pages.body:
## Symptom

Close the lid, reopen. Some panes are solid black. The caret still blinks, typing reaches the shell (the process sees it, and the output is in the buffer when you later force a repaint), but nothing paints. Only panes on the GPU renderer are affected; canvas panes are fine. On the 2019 16" MacBook Pro it happened almost every wake, on M-series almost never.

## Cause

macOS migrates the process between the discrete and integrated GPU on wake, and WKWebView drops the WebGL context. The browser fires `webglcontextlost`; addon 0.16 registered no listener, so the renderer kept issuing draw calls into a dead context. WebGL does not throw for this — the calls are quietly ignored — so there was no error anywhere, in any log.

Two things made it look like an input bug instead of a drawing bug. The compositor does not repaint while the display is asleep, so nothing forces a redraw until the user types; and the buffer is intact, so "scroll up and back" fixes some panes by accident when the scroll triggers a full repaint through the other code path.

## Handler

`webglcontextlost` → `preventDefault()` (without it the browser never attempts a restore at all) → dispose the addon → re-attach on `webglcontextrestored`, or after a 250 ms timer if the event never comes → `term.refresh(0, rows - 1)`. Three losses inside 60 s pins the pane to canvas and writes the reason to the renderer log. Unplugging an external GPU dock produces the identical event sequence and is covered by the same handler.

pages.title: Jump-to-previous-prompt lands on the wrong row after a resize because we stored absolute buffer coordinates
pages.body:
## Symptom

Cmd-Up ("go to previous prompt") lands N rows above or below the actual prompt once the user has narrowed the window. N grows with how many long lines sit in scrollback, and it never recovers — every further resize makes it worse.

## Cause

We recorded prompt positions as the absolute buffer Y at the moment the shell sent `OSC 133;A`. xterm rewraps the scrollback whenever the column count changes: a 200-character line takes 2 rows at 120 columns and 3 at 80, and every row beneath it shifts. An absolute Y is meaningless after the first resize.

Why it survived review and manual testing: rewrap only runs on the normal buffer, never on the alternate one. Anyone who tested inside vim, or with tmux attached, or in a pane that had never left full-screen mode, saw zero drift.

## Fix

Store `term.registerMarker()` handles instead of numbers — xterm rebases markers during rewrap for free. The catch the API docs bury: a marker is disposed when its line is trimmed out of scrollback, so the command-history list has to check `marker.isDisposed` and drop the entry rather than assume it can still be addressed. That check is the reason history entries silently disappear on very long sessions, which is intended.

We also debounce resize at 80 ms: rewrapping a 10 000-line buffer measured 380-420 ms, and a live window drag fired it a hundred times. Related: the scrollback cap that bounds that cost is [[render-scrollback-cap]].

pages.title: Scrollback is capped at 10 000 lines per pane and the real history lives in a tee'd file, not in the buffer
pages.body:
## The number and where it comes from

10 000 lines per pane. Measured at 200 columns with a full buffer, a pane costs 26 MB of resident memory for the buffer alone. Eight panes is about 210 MB, already more than the rest of the application put together, and the workspace layouts people actually build top out around eight.

## Rejected

*Unlimited* (`scrollback: Infinity`): a single `find / -type f` fills roughly 4 GB in 90 seconds and the app gets OOM-killed on a 16 GB machine. This is not theoretical, it is how the cap got prioritised.

*Scrollback in the session SQLite database*: attractive because it would survive restarts and reuse the sync path, but the session DB is fsynced at every workspace checkpoint. Teeing PTY output through it dropped a `cat` of a large file from 40 MB/s to 6 MB/s and produced 300 MB WAL files that the checkpointer never caught up with.

## What we do instead

The PTY reader tees raw bytes — escape sequences included, so the file can be replayed rather than just read — to a rotating per-pane file in the workspace directory, 32 MB × 4 files. Scrollback search reads that file, not the terminal buffer. That is why search can return lines you can no longer scroll to, which reads as a bug and is not one: the buffer is the fast path, the file is the record. The cap also bounds rewrap cost on resize ([[render-reflow-marker-drift]]).

pages.title: How a theme colour reaches a pixel: 16 slots, a generated 256 cube, and programs that overwrite both
pages.body:
## The path

A theme JSON becomes an `ITheme` — the sixteen named ANSI slots plus foreground, background, caret and selection — and that is handed to the terminal instance. Indices 16..255 of the 256-colour space are *generated* from the standard 6×6×6 cube and the 24 greys; a theme cannot restyle them. This is the single most common theming complaint we get: a TUI that paints itself in 256-colour indices (k9s, lazygit, most Go TUIs) looks identical under every theme we ship, and there is nothing wrong with the theme.

## minimumContrastRatio

Defaults to 1, meaning off. Set to 4.5 it makes the renderer compute an adjusted foreground per (fg, bg) pair and memoise it. That cache lives with the renderer and is dropped whenever the glyph texture is dropped, so the first repaint after a theme switch costs roughly 3x a normal one. It also visibly overrides colours a user chose on purpose, which is why it sits under accessibility settings rather than inside themes.

## Dim and runtime overrides

SGR 2 (dim) is drawn by blending the foreground 50% toward the background, and that blend happens *after* contrast adjustment — so dim text can sit below the ratio you asked for. Known, accepted, documented here so nobody re-files it.

Any program can rewrite a slot at runtime with OSC 4/10/11; vim colourschemes and some prompt frameworks do. Those overrides live in the terminal instance and outlive a theme switch until the program resets them or the pane is recreated. Distinct from, and often confused with, [[render-atlas-theme-invalidation]].

pages.title: Мыло на Windows при масштабе 125%: ячейку округляли в CSS-пикселях, а не в физических
pages.body:
## Симптом

Windows, системный масштаб 125% или 150%: текст мыльный, вертикальные штрихи букв разной толщины, при прокрутке строки будто дрожат. На 100% и 200% всё чётко. На macOS не воспроизводится вообще.

## Причина

`devicePixelRatio` = 1.25. Ширина ячейки считается в CSS-пикселях и получается дробной: 8.4 px, то есть 10.5 физических. Мы округляли CSS-размер, а физический оставался дробным, поэтому каждая вторая колонка начиналась на половине физического пикселя и растр глифа интерполировался при выводе.

На GPU-пути это хуже, чем на canvas: глиф растрируется один раз и кладётся в текстуру, а затем одна и та же ошибка выборки размножается по всей сетке одинаково — глаз читает это как системную нерезкость, а не как случайное сглаживание.

## Что сделали

Округляем ширину и высоту ячейки вниз до целого числа физических пикселей, сетку считаем от них, а остаток (обычно 2-4 px) отдаём правому и нижнему полю панели. Поле заметно, если специально искать; мыло замечали все.

Отдельная засада: WebView2 меняет raster scale при переносе окна между мониторами с разным DPI, но события `resize` при этом не приходит и размеры в CSS-пикселях не меняются. Подписываемся на `matchMedia('(resolution: 1.25dppx)')` и пересчитываем сетку по его срабатыванию. На macOS backing scale всегда 1 или 2, поэтому проблемы там нет и не будет.

pages.title: The first pane of a session gets a column count one too high because we measured before the bundled font loaded
pages.body:
## Symptom

In the first pane of a fresh session, full-screen programs (vim, htop, fzf) draw one column past the right edge and leave a ragged strip of leftover characters down the side. Any resize — even by one pixel — fixes it permanently. Every later pane in the same window is fine from the start.

## Cause

Cell width comes from rendering a run of `W` glyphs in the terminal font into a hidden span and dividing. On a cold start the bundled face is not in the document's font set yet, so that measurement silently falls back to the generic monospace face: 8.0 px instead of 8.4 px at 14 px type. `cols = floor(paneWidth / cellWidth)` then over-counts by one on a 1000 px pane, and we hand that wrong number to the PTY in the initial window-size ioctl. The program believes it has 121 columns; the renderer draws 120. The resize "fix" works because by then the font has loaded and the measurement is redone.

## The trap

`document.fonts.ready` is not sufficient and looks like it should be. It resolves when no font load is *pending* — and a face declared in CSS but not yet used by any rendered node was never requested, so the promise resolves immediately with the font absent. You must explicitly request each weight you draw with, `document.fonts.load('14px "JetBrains Mono"')` and the same for 700, and await both before opening the terminal. Later panes worked only because the first pane had already forced the load.

pages.title: Скрытые панели больше не рисуются: парсер работает, кадры не выдаются
pages.body:
## Проблема

Рабочее пространство с 12 панелями агентов, каждая пишет вывод, на экране одна. 140% CPU на M1 Pro при полностью неподвижном интерфейсе, вентилятор, разряд батареи за полтора часа. В профиле около 70% времени — рендер панелей, которых никто не видит.

Важная деталь, из-за которой это вообще случилось: Chromium сам душит `requestAnimationFrame` в скрытых вкладках, и мы на это рассчитывали. Но все наши панели живут в одном видимом документе — у нас собственная панель вкладок, для браузера каждая панель просто перекрыта другим элементом. Никакая автоматика не срабатывает, и не сработает.

## Решение

Панель вне экрана продолжает читать PTY и писать в буфер. Парсер отключать нельзя ни при каких условиях: escape-последовательности имеют состояние, пропущенный байт ломает разбор всего дальнейшего вывода. Отключается только выдача кадров — GPU-аддон не уничтожается, просто перестаёт получать вызовы отрисовки. При показе один полный `refresh(0, rows-1)`, 4-11 мс, заметно как лёгкая задержка при переключении вкладки. Стало 25% CPU на той же нагрузке.

## Отклонённые варианты

Снизить частоту скрытых панелей до 4 fps — почти не помогло: дорог сам полный кадр, а не их количество. Приостановить чтение PTY — обратное давление доходит до агента, он блокируется на записи и через минуту падает по таймауту; это мы уже проходили в оркестраторе.

pages.title: We own the column-width table for every codepoint, and disagreeing with the remote shell by one breaks the line
pages.body:
## Why this is our problem at all

Every cell is one or two columns wide. The program on the other end of the PTY — bash, ncurses, vim — decides the same thing independently with its own `wcwidth`. If the two answers differ by one for a single character, everything after it on that line is offset and cursor addressing goes wrong. Nobody reports it as a width problem; they report "editing a line leaves garbage behind" or "the caret is one to the left".

## Where the disagreements actually are

- **East Asian Ambiguous** (arrows, box drawing, `×`): one column in most Linux locales, two under CJK locales. We always answer one. A user with `LANG=ja_JP.UTF-8` gets drift in box-drawn TUIs and has to set the width mode in settings; there is no way to detect the remote locale from the client.
- **Emoji with VS16**: `✔` U+2714 followed by U+FE0F is two columns by UTS 51 and we honour it. glibc's `wcwidth` ignores variation selectors entirely and answers one. Over ssh to a Linux box we are simply wrong from its point of view, and the fix does not exist on our side.
- **ZWJ sequences** (👨‍👩‍👧): one grapheme, we draw two columns; most shells count each component separately, so they think six.

## What we pin

The unicode11 addon, patched forward to Unicode 15.1 tables. Mode 2027 (grapheme-cluster width) is deliberately not implemented: it only helps if the other side negotiates it too, and essentially nothing in the wild does.

pages.title: How to tell which draw path a pane ended up on and pin it to another one for a reproduction
pages.body:
## Find out what a pane is using

- **Overlay**: Ctrl+Shift+G toggles a per-pane heads-up display — draw path in use, current fps, p95 frame time, glyph texture pages live, and the count of dropped drawing contexts since the pane opened. It is the fastest answer and it is safe to ask a user to send a screenshot of it.
- **Console**: `window.__zenith.panes` in devtools returns `{id, renderer, cols, rows, fontLoaded}` per pane. Devtools is Cmd-Opt-I in dev builds; in a shipped build you need `ZENITH_DEVTOOLS=1` in the environment before launch.
- **Log**: every demotion is written once per pane to `~/Library/Logs/Zenith/renderer.log` on macOS or `%LOCALAPPDATA%\Zenith\logs\renderer.log` on Windows, with a reason string — `context-lost`, `atlas-overflow`, or `init-failed`. If a user says "it got slow after a while", this file is the first thing to ask for.

## Force one

`terminal.renderer` accepts `auto`, `webgl`, `canvas`, `dom`. It is read **once, when the pane is created** — changing the setting does not migrate open panes, so a user who "changed it and nothing happened" simply needs a new pane. For a clean reproduction across every pane including ones the agent orchestrator opens, launch with `ZENITH_FORCE_CANVAS=1`, which overrides the setting everywhere.

`dom` exists only for the accessibility snapshot tests. It is 5-10x slower and drops input under sustained output. Never hand it to a user as a workaround.

pages.title: Child reaping is driven by a SIGCHLD handler writing to a self-pipe, not by a polling loop
pages.body:
## Why a signal instead of a poll

The first PTY supervisor called `waitpid(-1, WNOHANG)` every 250 ms. Two measurable problems. Exit latency was visible: a pane stayed badged "running" for up to a quarter second after the user typed `exit`, which reads as lag even though nothing is actually slow. And on a 40-pane workspace the poll woke the supervisor thread about 160 times a second to do nothing, which showed up as 1.8% idle CPU on a MacBook Air — enough that it made the battery-drain triage list.

We now install a `SIGCHLD` handler that writes a single byte into a self-pipe registered with the mio poll set. The supervisor drains the pipe and loops `waitpid(-1, WNOHANG)` until it returns 0, so coalesced signals do not lose exits.

## Rejected: pidfd

`pidfd_open` plus epoll is race-free and much nicer to reason about, but it needs Linux 5.3, and several enterprise customers pin Ubuntu 20.04 images we still have to run on. macOS has nothing equivalent — kqueue `EVFILT_PROC` is close but its semantics across `exec` differ enough that we would maintain two genuinely different reap paths. One path for both Unixes was worth more than the elegance.

## Constraint on the handler

The handler must stay async-signal-safe: one `write(2)`, nothing else. An early draft called `tracing::debug!` from inside it and deadlocked when the signal landed on a thread that already held the tracing subscriber's lock. Reproduced roughly once per 500 pane closes; do not add logging there.

pages.title: Reaping moved to one blocking waitpid thread per child after the global SIGCHLD handler swallowed other crates' subprocesses
pages.body:
## What broke

A `SIGCHLD` handler is process-global, and our reaper called `waitpid(-1, ...)`, so it collected the exit status of children Zenith never spawned. Two victims: `git2`'s credential-helper shell-out, and the updater's `codesign --verify` subprocess. Both wait on their own children, both started getting `ECHILD` back because our reaper had already consumed the status. User-visible symptom was "update signature could not be verified" on about 3% of macOS auto-updates in 1.14.2, plus intermittent auth failures on private git remotes. A library that spawns and waits for its own child has no way to opt out of a process-wide handler, so this is not fixable by being careful about which pids we care about — by the time the handler runs, the status is gone.

## The replacement

Each spawned PTY child gets its own thread that blocks in `waitpid(pid, 0)` and pushes the result onto the same mpsc channel the old reaper fed, so everything downstream is unchanged. Threads are created with `stack_size(64 * 1024)`; at our 60-pane ceiling that is under 4 MB resident, measured, which we accepted rather than reintroduce a global handler. `SIGCHLD` is left at `SIG_DFL`.

## Do not optimise this back

The obvious cleanup is a single thread doing `waitpid(-1, 0)`. That has exactly the defect above — it reaps foreign children. Waiting on a specific pid is the whole point of the design, not an oversight. If thread count ever becomes a real problem, the correct move is per-platform (`pidfd` on new Linux, `EVFILT_PROC` on macOS), not a shared wait.

pages.title: PTY children inherit the entire Tauri process environment minus a six-name blocklist
pages.body:
## Why wholesale inheritance

When Zenith is started from a terminal (`zenith .`), the environment the app was given is exactly what the user expects to see inside a pane: their `SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, their `http_proxy`, whatever `direnv` exported in the directory they launched from, a `KUBECONFIG` pointing at the cluster they were already working against. Copying it verbatim into the child is the least-surprise behaviour and costs nothing.

## The blocklist

The host process is a WebKit/GTK application and injects variables that actively break child processes. We strip six before spawn: `WEBKIT_DISABLE_COMPOSITING_MODE`, `GDK_BACKEND`, `GIO_MODULE_DIR`, `APPDIR`, `ARGV0`, and `LD_LIBRARY_PATH`. The last is the important one — the AppImage runtime rewrites it to point at its bundled libraries, and any child that links the system `libstdc++` then fails with a `GLIBCXX_3.4.29 not found` error that looks like a broken machine rather than a broken terminal. On top of the strip we always set `TERM=xterm-256color`, `TERM_PROGRAM=Zenith`, and `TERM_PROGRAM_VERSION`.

## Rejected: build the environment from an allowlist

A clean-slate environment assembled from a fixed allowlist was prototyped for two nightlies. It is defensible on paper — reproducible, no surprises from the host — and it was withdrawn within 48 hours. The allowlist can never be complete: agent forwarding, corporate proxies, `direnv`, `asdf`, `NIX_PATH`, and vendor-specific tooling variables all vanished, and each one produced a bug report that read as "the terminal is broken" rather than "a variable is missing".

pages.title: The child environment is rebuilt from a one-time login-shell snapshot because launchd hands GUI apps a stub PATH
pages.body:
## The failure inheritance cannot fix

Launched from the Dock or Finder, macOS gives the app the launchd environment: `PATH=/usr/bin:/bin:/usr/sbin:/sbin`, and essentially nothing else. An ordinary shell pane papers over this, because the user's own rc files rebuild `PATH` when the interactive shell starts. The agent orchestration layer does not — it execs coding agents directly, with no shell in between, so those children got the stub path verbatim and died with `node: command not found` while a normal pane in the same window worked fine. 112 reports in the 1.19 cycle, the single most common issue of that release, and every one of them looked like an agent bug rather than an environment bug.

## What we do now

On first spawn we run `$SHELL -l -i -c 'export -p'` once, with a 4 second timeout, parse the result, and cache it in the workspace SQLite file keyed by shell path and mtime. The child environment is that snapshot, overlaid with the live parent values for variables that must stay current (`SSH_AUTH_SOCK`, `DISPLAY`, `WAYLAND_DISPLAY`, `XDG_RUNTIME_DIR`, `TERM*`), minus the WebKit blocklist inherited from [[pty-env-inherit-full-parent]].

## What it costs

The snapshot adds 120–400 ms to the first pane of a cold session; zsh with oh-my-zsh measured 380 ms at p50 on an M1. We block the first spawn on it rather than starting with the stub and swapping later, because a pane that changes its own `PATH` halfway through is worse than a pane that opens slowly. `ZENITH_ENV_SNAPSHOT=0` skips it for users with pathological rc files, and the cache is invalidated whenever the shell binary or the snapshot is older than 24 hours.

pages.title: A pane reports 128+signal for a killed child, which makes a genuine exit code of 137 indistinguishable from SIGKILL
pages.body:
## The encoding

`std::process::ExitStatus` on Unix wraps the raw wait status. `.code()` returns `None` when `WIFSIGNALED` is true, because a signalled process has no exit code at all. Our IPC contract to the frontend carries a single `u16`, so the PTY layer flattens with `code.unwrap_or(128 + signal)` — the same convention `$?` uses in every POSIX shell, chosen so that copying a number out of the pane and searching for it gives the user the answers they expect.

## Where the encoding lies

A process that calls `exit(137)` itself is indistinguishable from one killed by SIGKILL. This is not hypothetical: `docker run` propagates a container's OOM-kill as its own exit code 137, so our "killed by SIGKILL" badge blamed Zenith for kills that happened inside the container, and we spent two support cycles on it. Since 1.21 `PaneExit` carries a separate `signalled: bool` and the badge reads that flag instead of guessing from the number.

The numeric field kept the 128+N encoding anyway. The session-history table `pane_exits.code INTEGER` had roughly two years of rows written under the old meaning, and a migration would have had to invent information that was never recorded. New consumers should read `signalled` and treat the number as display text.

## Windows

None of this applies there — ConPTY children have no signals and exit codes go wrong in a completely different way; see [[pty-conpty-exit-259-still-active]].

pages.title: On Windows a pane whose program returned 259 hung forever, because 259 is STILL_ACTIVE
pages.body:
## Symptom

Windows only. A pane would never show its exit banner: the tab stayed live, the workspace row stayed `running`, and closing the window left `OpenConsole.exe` behind. Reproduced in three lines of Python (`sys.exit(259)`), but it was found in the wild by a customer whose MSBuild wrapper script returns the number of compiler warnings as its exit status. That build usually emits a couple of hundred warnings, so they hit it perhaps once a fortnight and could never say what was different about the runs that hung.

## Cause

`GetExitCodeProcess` overloads a single return value. It yields `STILL_ACTIVE` (259) for a process that is still running, and it yields 259 for a process that has finished with exit code 259. Our poll loop treated 259 as "not done yet" and looped forever. The documented Win32 discipline is to establish liveness separately: if `WaitForSingleObject(h, 0)` returns `WAIT_OBJECT_0` the process is dead, and only then is whatever `GetExitCodeProcess` reports a real exit code.

## Fix, and the handle that is easy to get wrong

`wait_windows()` now waits on the handle first and reads the code second. The subtlety worth writing down: the pseudoconsole handle is not a process handle. `CreatePseudoConsole` gives you nothing to wait on, so we retain `PROCESS_INFORMATION.hProcess` from the `CreateProcessW` call that was made with `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_PSEUDOCONSOLE`, and that is the handle the wait uses. Shipped in 1.17.3.

pages.title: Закрытие панели оставляло <defunct> процессы: поток ожидания создавался лениво
pages.body:
## Симптом

После часа активной работы `ps aux | grep defunct` показывал 40–60 зомби, родитель — PID Zenith. Память при этом не текла: запись в таблице процессов стоит около 1 КБ ядерной памяти и не растёт. Ломалось другое — пользователи macOS с дефолтным `kern.maxprocperuid` (1064) через день упирались в `fork: resource temporarily unavailable` при попытке открыть новую панель, и выглядело это как "приложение перестало открывать вкладки", без всякой связи с закрытыми ранее.

## Причина

Поток ожидания (см. [[pty-reap-dedicated-wait-thread]]) создавался лениво — в тот момент, когда фронтенд подписывался на событие выхода панели. Панель, закрытую пользователем, фронтенд отписывал ДО того, как Rust посылал SIGHUP. То есть для ребёнка, убитого при закрытии, `waitpid` не звал вообще никто: процесс умирал, ядро держало запись до выхода из приложения. Панели, где команда завершалась сама, никакого зомби не оставляли — поэтому баг не воспроизводился ни на одном нашем сценарии в CI.

## Что сделано

Поток ожидания теперь создаётся внутри `spawn()`, безусловно и до того, как pid попадёт куда-либо ещё; статус кладётся в `OnceLock`, а подписка фронтенда только читает готовое значение. Отписка больше ни на что не влияет. Тест `zombie_after_close` в `crates/pty/tests/lifecycle.rs` открывает и закрывает 200 панелей и через 2 секунды проверяет отсутствие детей: на Linux через `/proc/self/task/*/children`, на macOS через `proc_listchildpids`. Исправлено в 1.15.1.

pages.title: Перетаскивание сплиттера ломало отрисовку в nvim: TIOCSWINSZ вызывался на каждый кадр
pages.body:
## Симптом

При перетаскивании границы между панелями полноэкранные приложения — nvim, tmux, htop — рисовали мусор до тех пор, пока пользователь не нажмёт Ctrl-L. Изредка nvim падал с `Caught deadly signal SIGSEGV`. В трейсе видно до 140 вызовов `resize()` в секунду на одну панель.

## Причина

UI отправлял событие на каждый кадр анимации, а xterm.js пересчитывал cols/rows дважды за кадр — один раз из `ResizeObserver`, второй из `fit()`. Каждый такой вызов доходил до `ioctl(TIOCSWINSZ)`, а ядро на каждый ioctl шлёт SIGWINCH всей foreground process group. Приложения, которые читают размер в обработчике сигнала через `TIOCGWINSZ`, при такой частоте физически не успевают: пока идёт перерисовка по прочитанному размеру, размер уже другой, и буфер экрана расходится с реальностью. Падения — следствие того же: nvim пересобирает внутренние структуры окон под новый размер и на некоторых версиях 0.9.x не переживает повторный вход в этот код.

## Решение

Дебаунс сделан в Rust, а не в UI. `resize()` пишет упакованное значение (cols<<32|rows) в `AtomicU64` и будит таймер; сам ioctl выполняется не чаще одного раза в 16 мс и только если размер реально изменился по сравнению с последним отправленным. Trailing edge обязателен — без него финальный размер после отпускания мыши терялся, и панель оставалась с неверными cols до следующего ресайза. Почему именно в Rust: панели агентов меняют размер и без участия UI, когда оркестратор перекладывает layout, и этот путь не проходит через React вообще. На Windows дебаунс не применяется, там `ResizePseudoConsole` сам перерисовывает буфер ([[pty-conpty-vs-unix-pty-differences]]).

pages.title: ConPTY is a rendering server, not a pair of file descriptors, and that leaks into the whole PTY abstraction
pages.body:
## The shape mismatch

On Unix a PTY is two file descriptors with a kernel line discipline in between. The line discipline does echo, canonical mode, and signal generation — Ctrl-C becomes SIGINT delivered to the foreground process group, and none of that is our code. ConPTY (`CreatePseudoConsole`, Windows 10 1809 and later) is a different animal: you get two pipe handles and an out-of-process `OpenConsole.exe` that maintains a full screen buffer and re-emits VT sequences describing it.

Four consequences we live with:

- There is no line discipline to configure. `termios` has no analogue; raw mode is implicit and cannot be turned off.
- Ctrl-C is not a signal. We write `0x03` into the input pipe and conhost issues `GenerateConsoleCtrlEvent(CTRL_C_EVENT)` on our behalf — but only to processes attached to that pseudoconsole, and never to one that installed its own `SetConsoleCtrlHandler`.
- Resize is `ResizePseudoConsole`, it is synchronous, and it repaints: conhost re-emits the buffer. This is why the Unix debounce in [[pty-sigwinch-resize-coalescing]] is deliberately not applied on Windows.
- Output is reflowed by conhost before we ever see it, so byte-for-byte capture differs from Unix. Every pane-content snapshot test is `#[cfg(unix)]` for exactly this reason, and adding Windows goldens has been proposed and rejected twice.

## Why not winpty

winpty reaches back to Windows 7 and gives semantics closer to Unix by screen-scraping a hidden console. It costs an extra agent process per pane and mangles anything using the alternate screen buffer, which is most of what our users run. We dropped Windows 8.1 in 1.9 instead.

pages.title: Shell integration is injected through a per-pane rcfile trampoline, never by editing the user's dotfiles
pages.body:
## What is injected

OSC 133 prompt marks — `A` at prompt start, `B` at command start, `C` before execution, `D;<code>` when the command finishes — plus OSC 7 to report the working directory. Those four marks are what lets the UI find command boundaries for scrollback folding, re-run, and the "copy last output" action, and they are the only thing we add.

## How, per shell

- **zsh**: write `$XDG_RUNTIME_DIR/zenith-<pane>/.zshrc`, which sources the user's real `$ZDOTDIR/.zshrc` and then adds `precmd`/`preexec` hooks; spawn with `ZDOTDIR` pointed at that directory. Critically, the trampoline resets `ZDOTDIR` back to the original before sourcing, otherwise a user config containing `source $ZDOTDIR/.zshrc` recurses until the shell dies.
- **bash**: `--rcfile` for interactive non-login shells. Login bash ignores `--rcfile`, so there we set `PROMPT_COMMAND` in the environment instead — bash reads it after rc files run, which is late but correct.
- **fish**: prepend a directory containing `vendor_conf.d/zenith.fish` to `XDG_DATA_DIRS`.
- **nushell, powershell**: unsupported. `ZENITH_SHELL_INTEGRATION=0` disables everything.

## Why not install into the user's dotfiles

Other terminals offer a dotfile installer and inherit the support burden of stale lines left behind after uninstall. Our constraint is stronger than tidiness: an installed line contains a machine-specific absolute path, and a large share of our users keep `~/.zshrc` in a dotfiles repo shared across the very machines Zenith syncs between. The trampoline lives in tmpfs, is per-pane, and disappears with the process. It also composes with the snapshot in [[pty-env-login-shell-snapshot]], which must run against the unmodified config.

pages.title: Closing a pane walks SIGHUP, then SIGTERM, then SIGKILL over seven seconds, addressed to the process group
pages.body:
## The ladder

`killpg(pgid, SIGHUP)` immediately. If the child has not been reaped after 2 seconds, `SIGTERM`. After a further 5 seconds, `SIGKILL`, and we stop tracking it. Signals go to the process group, never to the bare pid. Signalling only the shell leaves everything it started — a `npm run dev`, an agent's `cargo watch` — alive, reparented to init, and still holding port 3000. That was the second most common complaint of the 1.12 beta, and it is why `setsid` in the child ([[pty-setsid-controlling-terminal]]) matters for teardown and not just for Ctrl-C.

## Why SIGHUP first

SIGHUP is what a real terminal hangup delivers, so shells already do the right thing with it: zsh runs `zshexit`, bash writes `~/.bash_history`. We shipped one nightly that opened with SIGTERM, and users lost shell history for every pane closed with the mouse — bash simply does not flush on SIGTERM. Starting with the signal the shell was designed to receive costs nothing and avoids inventing our own protocol.

## The timings, and the exception

2 seconds covers a zsh flushing a >100k-line `HISTFILE` with fsync, which measured ~700 ms at p99 on spinning disks. 5 seconds covers `docker compose` teardown of a small stack. Panes flagged `hold_on_exit` — agent panes whose output has not yet been collected — skip the ladder entirely and are killed only at app quit. Quitting runs the ladder for all panes in parallel with a hard 8 second cap, after which we exit regardless: macOS force-terminates an unresponsive app about 10 seconds into logout, and being killed mid-ladder is worse than exiting cleanly with one stubborn child left behind.

pages.title: Ctrl-C работает только потому, что ребёнок делает setsid() и TIOCSCTTY между fork и exec
pages.body:
## Что происходит между fork и exec

В дочернем процессе, до `execvp`, обязательны четыре шага в строгом порядке: `setsid()`; `ioctl(slave_fd, TIOCSCTTY, 0)`; `dup2` slave на дескрипторы 0, 1, 2; закрыть master и лишний slave. Порядок не косметический — `TIOCSCTTY` до `setsid()` возвращает EPERM, потому что процесс ещё не лидер сессии, а без `setsid()` ребёнок остаётся в сессии GUI-процесса, у которой управляющего терминала нет вовсе.

## Как выглядит поломка

Коварство в том, что всё внешне работает. Шелл стартует, приглашение рисуется, вывод идёт. Не работает только управление: Ctrl-C ничего не делает, `tty` в потомках печатает `not a tty`, `stty` падает с ENOTTY, bash при старте предупреждает `no job control in this shell`, а Ctrl-Z не сворачивает задачу. Причина одна — без управляющего терминала у ядра нет понятия foreground process group, и SIGINT слать некому. Из этого же следует и вся логика группового убийства при закрытии панели ([[pty-graceful-shutdown-sighup-sigterm-sigkill]]).

## Ограничение macOS

Между `fork()` и `exec()` в многопоточном процессе допустимы только async-signal-safe вызовы. Мы делаем эти шаги через `libc` напрямую и не используем замыкание `Command::pre_exec` с аллокациями: на macOS всё, что трогает malloc или Objective-C runtime после fork, может зависнуть намертво — `pthread_atfork` не приводит в порядок libdispatch. Реальный баг из 1.11: `CString::new` внутри pre_exec вешал спавн панели примерно один раз на 300 холодных стартов, и стек висящего потока был внутри `malloc_zone_malloc`.

pages.title: The tail of a fast command's output was dropped because the reader was torn down as soon as the child exited
pages.body:
## Symptom

A pane that ran something short and exited immediately sometimes showed nothing at all. Reproducible about one run in twenty with `printf 'x%.0s' {1..8000}; exit`, and reported by users as "output missing when the command finishes instantly". Never happened for long-running commands, which is why it survived so long — every manual test we had involved a shell that stayed alive.

## Cause

Two independent events race: the wait thread learns the child exited, and the reader thread drains the master fd. We closed the master as soon as the exit status arrived. The PTY buffer still held unread bytes, and closing the master discards them — the kernel makes no promise to flush. On macOS it was worse: the reader was blocked in `read()` and got `EBADF` from underneath it, so even bytes already available were lost.

Stacked on top of that, `read()` on a Linux master returns `EIO`, not 0, once the last slave descriptor closes. We classified `EIO` as a hard error, logged it, and dropped whatever was already buffered. Either bug alone would have caused truncation; together they made the loss look nondeterministic.

## Fix

The exit status is now held in the pane state and not published until the reader signals EOF. The reader treats `errno == EIO` on Linux as a clean end of stream. The master is closed only after the drain loop finishes or a 250 ms grace timer fires — the timer is necessary because a grandchild still holding the slave open (`nohup sleep 1000 &`) means EOF legitimately never arrives, and without it the pane would refuse to close.

pages.title: A pane stayed live after its shell died because a concurrent spawn inherited that pane's master fd
pages.body:
## Symptom

Rare, Linux only, and only when four or more panes were created inside the same second — in practice, restoring a saved workspace. One pane would never reach EOF. Its shell was long gone (`ps` showed nothing under that pid), but the tab stayed marked live, the close button did nothing, and quitting the app was the only way out. Roughly a dozen reports over six months, all with "restored a session" in the description, none reproducible on demand.

## Cause

A missing `O_CLOEXEC`. We opened the master with `posix_openpt(O_RDWR | O_NOCTTY)` and set `FD_CLOEXEC` afterwards with a separate `fcntl`. Between those two syscalls another thread could `fork` and `exec` for a different pane, and that unrelated child inherited pane A's master descriptor. As long as any process holds the master open, the slave side never sees a hangup, so pane A's reader blocks forever on a shell that no longer exists. The window is microseconds wide, which is why only a burst of concurrent spawns could hit it.

## Fix, and what does not fix it

`posix_openpt(O_RDWR | O_NOCTTY | O_CLOEXEC)` — supported by glibc since 2.9 and by musl from the start. Note that close-on-exec is not sufficient for the slave: the child deliberately keeps its own slave, so the pre-exec hook still walks `/proc/self/fd` on Linux and `proc_pidinfo` on macOS and closes everything above 2, which also catches descriptors leaked by dependencies we do not control. A global spawn mutex was proposed and rejected — it serialises workspace restore, which measured 340 ms for 12 panes and would have become roughly 1.2 s.

pages.title: OpenConsole.exe survived app quit until every Windows child was created inside a kill-on-close job object
pages.body:
## Symptom

Windows only. After a few days of continuous use, Task Manager showed 20–80 `OpenConsole.exe` processes at roughly 6 MB each, plus the occasional orphaned `node.exe` still holding a listening socket. Quitting Zenith did not clear them; only a reboot did. Two enterprise users on Citrix hit their per-user process quota because of it and could not start new sessions at all, which is how it got prioritised.

## Cause

`ClosePseudoConsole` is documented to terminate the attached console host, but it blocks until the connected client has drained pending output. If the client is already dead in a way that leaves the output pipe unread, the call returns after our 500 ms timeout while conhost carries on living. Separately, Windows has no process groups: killing the shell leaves whatever it started with no relationship we can walk. Reconstructing a tree with `CreateToolhelp32Snapshot` and parent pids is not reliable, because Windows reuses pids aggressively and a recycled pid makes you kill an innocent process.

## Fix

Every spawn now goes into a per-pane Job Object with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`, assigned through `PROC_THREAD_ATTRIBUTE_JOB_LIST` at `CreateProcessW` time so there is no window in which the child exists outside the job. Closing the pane closes the job handle and the entire tree dies, console host included.

Caveat: a child that wants to create its own job — older Docker Desktop helpers, some MSI-based installers — fails under nested-job rules before Windows 10 1809. We already require 1809 for ConPTY itself ([[pty-conpty-vs-unix-pty-differences]]), so this costs us nothing.

pages.title: Pane layout is stored as one serialized document in workspaces.layout_json, not as rows
pages.body:
## What we picked

`workspaces.layout_json TEXT NOT NULL` holds the whole split tree — every node, its direction, its ratio, and the pane id at the leaves — produced by `serde_json::to_string` on the same struct the frontend already sends over IPC.

The alternative on the table was a `panes` table with `parent_id`/`ord` columns and a recursive CTE to reassemble the tree. Rejected in review for three reasons: the layout is always read and written whole (there is no "load pane 4 of 30" path anywhere in the app), a tree in SQL needs either recursive CTEs or an in-memory assembly step we would have to test on its own, and the frontend already owns the tree shape — a normalized schema would mean two definitions of the same structure drifting apart at every feature.

## What it costs us

Any change rewrites the entire document. A typical 8-pane workspace is ~4 KB; the largest one we found in dogfood dumps was 38 KB, and renaming a single tab rewrites all of it.

Nothing inside a pane is queryable. "Which workspace has a pane sitting in ~/src/zenith" is a scan-and-parse loop in Rust, not a WHERE clause.

Sync, when it lands, will have to reconcile opaque text rather than fields.

We accepted all three knowingly: at 12 workspaces per user (p95 in telemetry) none of it is measurable today.

pages.title: Layout moved to normalized pane rows after whole-document rewrites made sync merges destructive
pages.body:
## Why the document had to go

Sync made the cost real. Two machines with the same workspace open, one resizes a split and the other renames a tab: both write `layout_json`, and the merge sees a single column changed on both sides. Field-level reconciliation is impossible on a serialized blob, so last-writer-wins silently discarded the other machine's edit. Three people hit this in the first week of the sync alpha and all three filed it as "my panes jump back".

The write amplification we waved through in [[persist-layout-json-blob]] also stopped being theoretical: a 38 KB document rewritten at the end of every drag, multiplied by WAL page churn, was the single largest contributor to `-wal` growth on the dogfood builds.

## The shape now

`panes(id TEXT PK, workspace_id, parent_id, split_dir, ratio REAL, cwd, title, ord INTEGER)`, tree by `parent_id`, plus a materialized `depth` column with `CHECK (depth <= 12)` so a cycle introduced by a bad sync merge cannot hang the loader instead of failing it. Migration 0011 parses the old documents and backfills. It leaves `layout_json` in place, unread, until 0.14, so a user who rolls back still has something to open.

## The bill

Loading a 60-pane workspace is now three statements plus tree assembly: 1.8 ms against 0.3 ms before. Nobody can perceive it. In exchange sync diffs per row, and a resize on one machine no longer clobbers a rename on the other.

pages.title: journal_mode=DELETE everywhere, because the store lived in a home directory that could be on NFS
pages.body:
## Symptom

Enterprise Linux testers could not start Zenith at all: `unable to open database file` on first launch, every launch, on machines where `$HOME` came from an NFS automount. A smaller group of macOS reports said "my session is lost every restart" and carried `disk I/O error` from the same open path; those users had their config directory inside iCloud Drive or Dropbox.

## Cause

Write-ahead logging needs a shared-memory index — the `-shm` file — and SQLite maps it with `mmap`. NFS, SMB and most FUSE layers either refuse the mapping or give one without coherent locking, so the open fails with `SQLITE_IOERR_SHMOPEN`. The cloud-drive case has a different mechanism and the same root: the sync client rewrites `-wal` underneath the process, and SQLite finds a log that no longer matches the header it wrote.

## Decision

`PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE` unconditionally, on every platform, no runtime detection.

We prototyped a probe — `statfs.f_type` on Linux, `getattrlist` for `VOL_CAP_INT_REMOTE` on macOS — and threw it away: sshfs and rclone mounts report as local, so the probe answered "safe" exactly where it was not, and being wrong here means the app does not launch rather than launching slowly.

## Price

A rollback-journal commit fsyncs twice. Layout save p50 goes from 9 ms to 34 ms on 5400 rpm laptop disks, and a save blocks readers for its duration.

pages.title: Write-ahead logging is back on after the store moved out of $HOME into the OS state directory
pages.body:
## The reframing

Nothing about network filesystems got better. We stopped keeping the database somewhere a network filesystem can be. The store moved from the config directory to the platform state directory: `~/Library/Application Support/dev.zenith/state` on macOS, `$XDG_STATE_HOME` (default `~/.local/state`) on Linux, and on Windows explicitly `%LOCALAPPDATA%` — never `%APPDATA%`, since the roaming profile is the Windows analogue of the NFS home and gets copied over the network at logoff.

On the corporate images that produced the original reports, `~/.local/state` is on local disk by policy even when `$HOME` is not. That is the whole reason the reversal is possible; it is an assumption about somebody else's fleet, so it is written down here.

## Result

`journal_mode=WAL` plus `synchronous=NORMAL` ([[persist-synchronous-normal-tradeoff]]). Layout save p50 drops from 34 ms to 2 ms, and a read no longer waits behind a write, which is what makes the read-only connections in [[persist-single-writer-actor]] worth having.

## Guards kept from the old world

The filesystem probe survives, demoted: at open we check whether the resolved state path is remote, and if it looks like it is we log loudly and run that session in DELETE mode rather than failing. Being wrong now costs latency, not a launch.

The old database is copied, not moved. The original file stays where it was for one release so a downgrade still finds it; 0.15 deletes it.

pages.title: An older build opens a newer store read-only instead of trying to migrate downward
pages.body:
## The incident

Users who run stable and nightly side by side share one state directory, which is intentional — they want the same workspaces in both. Nightly shipped schema 14, which added `panes.agent_kind NOT NULL DEFAULT ''` and dropped a column stable still wrote. Stable read `PRAGMA user_version = 14`, saw that its own maximum was 12, concluded there was nothing to migrate, and carried on writing. Inserts failed on the missing column, the error path swallowed it as "save failed", and two people lost a week of workspaces because saving had been quietly off the whole time.

## Rule now

The store carries a `meta.min_reader_version` row alongside `user_version`. A build whose supported schema is below `min_reader_version` opens the connection read-only, restores workspaces normally, and shows a persistent banner saying session saving is disabled and which version to run. Nothing is written, nothing is destroyed, and the state is obvious instead of inferred from missing saves.

## What we rejected

Down-migrations. A migration that removes a column removes the data in it; writing 14→13 means deciding what to throw away, on a schema we already replaced, for a path taken by roughly the twenty people running two channels.

Separate stores per channel. Tried in a branch; it makes nightly useless for actual daily work, which is the only reason people run it.

See [[persist-migration-advisory-lock]] for the concurrency side of the same startup path.

pages.title: Две копии Zenith одновременно накатывали миграции и падали с database is locked
pages.body:
## Симптом

Zenith стоит в автозапуске, и на части машин при входе в систему окно не открывалось вовсе: через пять секунд после старта в логе `database is locked`, дальше выход. Воспроизводилось только на холодном старте и только там, где приложение поднималось дважды почти одновременно — агент автозапуска плюс восстановление сессии macOS после перезагрузки.

## Причина

Миграции шли по шагам, каждый шаг в своей транзакции, а `PRAGMA user_version` читался один раз до первого шага, вне транзакции записи. Оба процесса видели 12 и оба решали накатить 13 и 14. Первый брал блокировку на `ALTER TABLE`, второй ждал `busy_timeout` 5000 мс и падал.

Хуже был второй сценарий: если первый успевал закончить шаг 13 и отпустить блокировку раньше таймаута, второй накатывал тот же шаг повторно и получал `duplicate column name`. Это уже выглядело как повреждение схемы и один раз увело нас в отладку не туда.

## Что сделали

Вся цепочка идёт под одной `BEGIN IMMEDIATE`, а `user_version` перечитывается уже внутри неё. Проигравший процесс видит актуальную версию и просто ничего не делает. `busy_timeout` на время миграции поднят до 30 с — полный `VACUUM` в 0014 ([[persist-incremental-vacuum-idle]]) заведомо длиннее пяти секунд.

Отдельный lock-файл не заводили: SQLite и так даёт нужную взаимоисключимость, а файл пришлось бы подчищать после аварийного завершения — то есть решать ровно ту задачу, от которой уходили.

pages.title: Every store write goes through one Rust actor; the webview never opens the database
pages.body:
## The rule

Exactly one `Connection` in the process is open for writing, owned by the `SessionStore` actor — a thread holding an `mpsc::Receiver<StoreCmd>`, with no handle shared anywhere. The webview has no database access at all; React calls `invoke("save_layout", …)` and the command lands in that queue.

## Why not a small connection pool

Two reasons, and the second is the one people forget.

SQLite serializes writers regardless. A pool converts that serialization into `SQLITE_BUSY` which every call site then has to retry correctly.

Ordering. Tauri's `invoke` is request/response over an async channel, and completions are not ordered with respect to each other. Two `save_layout` calls issued 4 ms apart during a drag can be picked up in either order by two pool connections, and the older snapshot wins roughly one time in fifty. The user sees the split ratio snap back to its previous value when the mouse is released. A single consumer gives total order for free, and on top of that each layout command carries a monotonic sequence number so the actor can drop a snapshot older than the one already committed.

## Reads are not funnelled

With WAL in place ([[persist-wal-local-state-dir]]) two read-only connections serve the UI directly and never block the writer or each other. Only the write path is a queue. Plugins get the same treatment through the same actor, which is also how we keep arbitrary plugin SQL out of the store entirely.

pages.title: A clean exit deletes a marker row, so finding that row at startup means the last run died
pages.body:
## The mechanism

`runtime_state` holds one row, `session_open -> "<boot_id>:<pid>"`, written when the first window opens and deleted on the normal quit path after the final checkpoint. Its presence at startup is the crash signal.

The pid alone was not enough. After a reboot the kernel reuses pids freely, and a stale row pointing at pid 812 matched some unrelated live process often enough that we shipped a release in which crashes were essentially never detected. The value now carries a boot identifier as well — `kern.boottime` on macOS, `/proc/sys/kernel/random/boot_id` on Linux, boot time via `GetTickCount64` on Windows — and a row from an earlier boot counts as a crash with no process check at all.

## What changes downstream

After a clean exit the last committed layout is restored silently, panes in place, no question asked.

After a crash the layout is whatever survived the last checkpoint, which under `synchronous=NORMAL` ([[persist-synchronous-normal-tradeoff]]) can be a few seconds stale. That is why this case prompts instead of restoring: we are offering possibly-wrong state and saying so. It is also the only place we can tell the user the previous run died, without putting a dialog in the quit path.

Multiple windows share the single row — written by the first, cleared by the last — so closing one of three windows is not a crash, and killing the process with three windows open is.

pages.title: A damaged store is renamed aside and never deleted; Zenith starts on a fresh empty one
pages.body:
## Behaviour

`SQLITE_CORRUPT` or `SQLITE_NOTADB` on open, or a failing `PRAGMA quick_check` at startup, and the file is renamed to `sessions.corrupt-<unix-ts>.db` along with its `-wal` and `-shm`. A new empty database is created, the app opens with no workspaces, and a persistent banner names the quarantined path.

## Why not delete, and why not repair in place

Deleting was the behaviour for two releases. It ended when a user's antivirus rewrote the middle of a store holding about 200 workspaces: we would have thrown the file away, and instead we recovered 190 of them by hand with `sqlite3 .recover` on a copy they mailed us. Everything past the first damaged page was intact.

In-process repair was rejected because we cannot do it: the `recover` extension is not compiled into the bundled amalgamation we link ([[persist-bundled-sqlite-pin]]), and shipping the `sqlite3` CLI just to run `.recover` means another signed and notarized binary per platform for a path that fires for maybe one user in ten thousand.

## Housekeeping

At most three quarantine files are kept, oldest deleted first. With scrollback held outside the database ([[persist-scrollback-outside-sqlite]]) they are normally a few megabytes, but one store that swallowed a bad import reached 400 MB, which is why there is a cap at all.

pages.title: The -wal file reached 2.3 GB because the telemetry aggregator held a read transaction open forever
pages.body:
## Symptom

Two dogfood machines had `sessions.db-wal` at 2.3 GB and 1.7 GB beside a 40 MB database, and a cold start that spent 38 seconds before the first window appeared, because opening replays the log.

## Cause

A passive checkpoint can only copy frames older than the oldest live reader's snapshot. The telemetry aggregator opened a read transaction during startup to count workspaces, and then kept the `rusqlite::Rows` iterator alive in a struct field for the process lifetime. The statement was never finalized, so the transaction never ended, so the checkpointer could never advance past roughly frame 1200. Auto-checkpoint kept firing on schedule and kept copying nothing. There is no error and no log line for a checkpoint that legitimately does nothing, which is why this ran for six weeks.

`journal_size_limit=32MB` was already set and was irrelevant: truncation happens only after a checkpoint succeeds.

## Fix and the guard

Telemetry now collects into a `Vec` and drops the statement inside the same function; the aggregation happens on owned data.

Beyond the fix, a watchdog samples the `-wal` size every 60 s and, above 64 MB, logs the age of the oldest open read transaction and which subsystem opened it. The point is not the threshold, it is that a starved checkpointer is now observable without reproducing it locally.

pages.title: synchronous=NORMAL: a power cut may lose the last few seconds of layout, and that is fine
pages.body:
## Setting

`PRAGMA synchronous=NORMAL` together with WAL. Commits do not force the log to stable storage; that happens at checkpoints.

## Why

On macOS a full sync is `F_FULLFSYNC`, a genuine barrier down to the device: 8–12 ms per commit on an M2 and worse on the 2019 Intel machines in the test rack. Layout writes happen on every splitter release and every tab rename, so a drag ending in three commits was visibly janky and the profiler put all of it in the sync call.

With WAL and NORMAL the failure mode is bounded and precise: a power loss or kernel panic can lose transactions committed since the last checkpoint, but cannot leave a torn database. An application crash — by far the common case — loses nothing, because the log is already in the page cache and the kernel writes it out.

What we can lose is a few seconds of pane geometry and titles. Nothing in this store is authoritative for anything outside Zenith: user files are user files, agent transcripts are separate files ([[persist-agent-panes-restored-inert]]), settings live in TOML.

## The two exceptions

The updater, immediately before it relaunches, and the explicit Quit command both flip to `synchronous=FULL`, checkpoint with TRUNCATE, then commit. Those are exactly the moments where the machine may go down right behind us and where 10 ms is invisible.

pages.title: Скроллбэк панелей лежит в отдельных ring-файлах, а не в SQLite
pages.body:
## Решение

История вывода в базе не хранится. Каждой панели соответствует файл `state/scrollback/<pane-uuid>.ring` — кольцевой буфер фиксированного размера 8 МБ с 64-байтным заголовком: смещения головы и хвоста и номер первой строки. В SQLite от него остаются только имя файла и счётчик строк.

## Почему не BLOB

Посчитали на реальных дампах: 80 панелей по 10 000 строк — это 600–900 МБ. Сам SQLite это выдержит, incremental blob I/O даёт нормальный потоковый доступ, но перестаёт работать всё вокруг базы. Полный `VACUUM`, который нам понадобился в 0014 ([[persist-incremental-vacuum-idle]]), переписывает эти гигабайты целиком. Резервная копия перед миграцией — тоже. Page cache вымывается выводом команд вместо метаданных, и чтение layout начинает ходить на диск. Синхронизация между машинами гоняла бы терабайты в месяц ради текста, который никто не откроет.

## Чем платим

Два хранилища расходятся, и атомарности между ними нет. На старте GC удаляет ring-файлы, для которых нет строки в `panes`. Обратный случай — строка есть, файла нет — не считается ошибкой: панель открывается с пустой историей, прошлый вывод потерян.

Сделать атомарно значило бы писать скроллбэк той же транзакцией, что и layout, то есть коммитить каждые несколько килобайт вывода. Это ровно тот сценарий, ради которого мы отказались от fsync на коммит ([[persist-synchronous-normal-tradeoff]]).

pages.title: Restored agent panes come back as read-only transcripts and are never auto-respawned
pages.body:
## Rule

A restored workspace brings agent panes back inert. The pane is there, the scrollback is there, the working directory and the agent kind are there, and nothing is running. A Resume button relaunches with the recorded arguments. A human has to press it.

## Why the button exists

0.9 restored agent panes by re-executing the recorded command with `--resume`. A tester hit a crash loop — the renderer panicked on a malformed OSC sequence about ten seconds into each restore — and every restore relaunched four agents. Six cycles in four minutes, roughly $40 of tokens, and one agent got far enough to `git checkout` a branch and stomp uncommitted work.

The constraint is not ours to relax. Coding agents bill per token and they take side effects: they write files, run commands, push branches. Automatic restart after an event the user did not choose — a crash, a forced OS-update reboot — is a category of action that needs consent each time it happens.

## What is actually persisted

`panes.agent_kind`, `agent_argv` as JSON, `cwd`, `transcript_path`, and the exit reason.

Not the agent's own conversation state. That lives in the agent's own directory; we neither read nor copy it, which incidentally keeps API keys and prompt contents out of the store and therefore out of sync between machines.

pages.title: SQLite is compiled into the binary because distro system libraries were too old for RETURNING
pages.body:
## The constraint

We use `INSERT … ON CONFLICT … RETURNING` (SQLite 3.35, March 2021) and `STRICT` tables (3.37). Debian bullseye ships 3.34. Ubuntu 20.04 — at the time the most common Linux in our crash reports — ships 3.31. RHEL 8 is on 3.26.

Linking the system library meant those users installed cleanly, launched cleanly, and got `near "RETURNING": syntax error` the first time they opened a workspace. A failure at the worst possible moment for diagnosis, and completely invisible to CI, which builds on a current image.

## Decision

`libsqlite3-sys` with the `bundled` feature, pinned to 3.45.x, the same build on every platform. macOS included: the system copy there is also behind, and Apple patches it in ways we cannot test against.

## What it costs

Distro security updates to SQLite no longer reach our users. A SQLite CVE is now a release we have to cut ourselves, which is why it sits on the dependency review checklist rather than being assumed handled by the platform.

The build needs a C toolchain, which is what broke the Windows runner for a day until the image gained the MSVC build tools.

Binary size grows about 1.4 MB.

One knock-on effect worth knowing: the amalgamation we compile does not include the `recover` extension, which is why [[persist-corrupt-db-quarantine]] quarantines rather than repairs.

pages.title: Файл базы не уменьшался после удаления воркспейсов, пока её не пересоздали с auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL
pages.body:
## Симптом

База 380 МБ при двенадцати живых воркспейсах. Удаление воркспейса освобождало строки, но файл не уменьшался ни на байт. У одного пользователя он дорос до 1.2 ГБ за полгода, и первым подозреваемым был скроллбэк — хотя он в базе не лежит вовсе ([[persist-scrollback-outside-sqlite]]).

## Причина

`auto_vacuum` задаётся только до создания первой таблицы. Все базы, созданные до 0.11, стоят в режиме `NONE`: освобождённые страницы уходят во freelist и переиспользуются при следующих вставках, но файл не усекается никогда. Задним числом прагма записывается молча и без эффекта — она вступает в силу только после полного `VACUUM`, который переписывает файл целиком.

## Что сделали

Миграция 0014 один раз выполняет `PRAGMA auto_vacuum=INCREMENTAL; VACUUM;`. Это не транзакционно, блокирует запись (6 с на 380 МБ на SSD) и требует свободного места примерно вдвое больше размера базы. Поэтому миграция сначала проверяет свободное место и при нехватке пропускает шаг до следующего запуска, а не падает — иначе пользователь с забитым диском получил бы приложение, которое не стартует, вместо приложения с большим файлом.

Дальше при простое раз в пять минут вызывается `incremental_vacuum(200)`. 200 страниц — это около 800 КБ, укладывается в один кадр и не даёт заметной паузы в UI.

pages.title: An agent pane is allocated and focused before the process forks, and buffers input until run_ready arrives
pages.body:
## Why the pane exists before the process

Spawning is deliberately two-phase. `spawn.ts` allocates a pane id and inserts the `agent_run` row *before* the supervisor forks anything; the Rust side answers with `run_ready { run_id, pid, cwd }`. Until that message lands the pane renders an xterm bound to a null sink — normally 300-700ms, dominated by `git worktree add` (see [[agents-worktree-per-run]]).

The ordering is not cosmetic. The first thing people do after clicking "Run agent" is start typing the instruction. In 0.6 the pane only appeared once the fork succeeded, and focus stayed wherever it was: we got 11 reports of half-typed prompts landing in a live shell, one of which was submitted as a command. Keystrokes now go into a 4KB pending buffer and are replayed into the PTY on `run_ready`.

## The handshake

Three messages, all over the Tauri event channel, all carrying `run_id` (never pane index — panes get reordered by drag):

1. `run_requested` (UI to Rust) — cwd, model, instruction, workspace id
2. `run_ready` (Rust to UI) — pid and the resolved working directory, which may differ from the requested one
3. `run_exit` — exit code, reason enum (`completed`, `cancelled`, `interrupted`, `denied`)

If `run_ready` does not arrive within 15s the pane shows a failure card rather than hanging; the supervisor is still asked to reap, because a slow worktree add can succeed after we gave up.

## Gotcha

`run_exit` is not the same as the pane closing. A pane can be detached while the process lives — that path is documented in [[agents-pane-crash-transcript-recovery]].

pages.title: Simultaneous agent runs are capped at a hard 4; a load-average scheduler was tried and rejected as unpredictable
pages.body:
## The number

Four. Not per-core, not configurable in the UI, only `agents.maxParallel` in settings.json for people who insist. A fifth request queues and the pane shows "waiting for a slot".

## Why not scale with the machine

We shipped a scheduler in the 0.9 betas that admitted runs while the 1-minute load average stayed under `ncpu * 0.7`. It oscillated badly. An agent run is bursty — idle while waiting on the model, then a `cargo check` that saturates every core for 40 seconds — so the load average lagged the real state by roughly a minute. The scheduler admitted three runs into a lull, all three hit their build step together, and on a 16-core desktop we ended up with 12 concurrent runs and a compositor at 12fps. Testers described it as "the app decides at random how slow it wants to be today", which is worse than a limit that is merely wrong.

The floor case decided the constant. On an 8GB M1 Air each run costs roughly 600MB RSS for the agent process plus whatever the project's toolchain does; four runs plus the app plus a browser is already at the swap boundary. Going lower made the feature pointless for the people who actually want parallel agents.

## Accepted cost

Owners of 64GB workstations get four slots and nothing more. We took that knowingly: predictable and mildly wasteful beat adaptive and jittery. Revisit only if we can measure memory *pressure* rather than CPU load.

pages.title: Admission control reads host memory pressure instead of a fixed run count, with a floor of 1 and a ceiling of 8
pages.body:
## What changed

The constant is gone. Before admitting a run the supervisor samples a pressure signal and admits while the 10-second average sits under 20%:

- macOS: `host_statistics64` + the `kern.memorystatus_vm_pressure_level` sysctl
- Linux: `/proc/pressure/memory` `some avg10`
- Windows: commit charge from `GlobalMemoryStatusEx`, normalised against the commit limit

Sampling is every 2s; admission needs two consecutive clean samples so a single `cargo build` spike does not gate a run. Floor is 1 (we always let one run start, even under pressure — refusing entirely reads as a broken app), ceiling is 8 to keep the approval broker and the transcript writers sane.

## Why the old cap died

Two numbers from the 1.2 telemetry. 62% of runs happened on machines with 32GB or more, where four slots left most of the box idle and users were opening a second copy of the app to get around it — which defeated the limit completely. At the other end, 8GB machines still swapped at four runs, so the constant was simultaneously too low and too high.

The reason we can do now what we could not do in 0.9 is that we stopped watching CPU. Memory pressure is a *level*, not a rate, so it does not lag behind bursty work the way load average did.

## Rejected

Per-run cgroup v2 limits, which would have been stricter and cheaper to reason about, but there is no equivalent on macOS and we were not shipping two different resource models.

pages.title: Every agent run gets a detached git worktree; containers were rejected because the user's toolchain lives outside the repo
pages.body:
## The mechanism

`git worktree add --detach .zenith/wt/<run-id> HEAD`, one per run, removed on exit plus a sweep at app start. The sweep exists because `git worktree prune` only removes administrative files — it leaves build output, `target/`, and anything the agent wrote that git never tracked, and we had a tester sitting on 41GB of abandoned `.zenith/wt`.

We require git >= 2.38. Older versions race when two `worktree add` calls run concurrently against the same repo and can leave a half-written entry in `.git/worktrees`, which then poisons every later `git status` in the main checkout.

## Why not containers

The obvious answer was a devcontainer per run, and it does not survive contact with how people actually configure machines. Toolchains are installed by `mise`/`asdf` under `$HOME`, signing identities live in the macOS keychain, and half our early users work on repos whose test suite talks to a service running on the host. Every one of those becomes a bind mount or a broken build, and on macOS the VM layer added 4-6s of startup and made file watching unreliable.

## Why not one shared checkout

Tried first, because it is trivial. Two agents editing the same file overwrote each other within minutes, and worse, they overwrote the *user's* unsaved work — the human's editor and the agents were pointed at the same paths. File locks only converted that into deadlocks between agents that were each waiting for the other to finish a refactor.

Merging back is deliberately manual: the run ends with a diff the user applies. Auto-merge is a separate problem and we did not solve it here.

pages.title: Тесты агента писали файлы в основной чекаут: symlink на node_modules уводил vitest за пределы воркtree
pages.body:
## Симптом

Сначала было простое: в свежем worktree нет `node_modules`, агент получал `Cannot find module 'vitest'` и сам запускал `pnpm install` — 40+ секунд и ~300МБ на каждый запуск, при четырёх параллельных агентах диск умирал.

Очевидный фикс — симлинк `node_modules` из основного чекаута — сломал всё тише и хуже. Vitest резолвит конфиг и корень проекта через `fs.realpath`. Пройдя по симлинку, он оказывался в `/repo/node_modules/...`, поднимался вверх до `/repo` и считал корнем основной чекаут. Снапшоты, `__mocks__` и всё, что тест писал через относительные пути, приземлялось в рабочую копию пользователя. Один агент таким образом переписал снапшоты в ветке, которую человек в этот момент правил руками.

## Причина

pnpm раскладывает `node_modules` как симлинки в общий стор `node_modules/.pnpm`. То есть даже «настоящий» `node_modules` внутри воркtree — это ссылки наружу; вопрос был только в том, на какой уровень уходит realpath.

## Что сделали

Симлинкуем только стор (`node_modules/.pnpm`), а сам `node_modules` создаём внутри воркtree через `pnpm install --offline --frozen-lockfile`. Стор уже прогрет, установка занимает ~1.8с. Корень проекта при этом настоящий, realpath никуда не уводит.

`--preserve-symlinks` у Node отвергли: он чинит резолвинг, но ломает пакеты, которые сравнивают пути по идентичности, и его нельзя включить для дочерних процессов, которые агент запускает сам.

Для Cargo сделали проще — общий `CARGO_TARGET_DIR`, у него нет аналогичной проблемы с корнем.

pages.title: Agent output pinned the UI thread at ~9k IPC events/s until deltas were coalesced into 16ms frames in Rust
pages.body:
## What we saw

One agent running `cargo build --verbose` made the whole window unusable: typing latency over 400ms, scrolling at single-digit fps, and the fan audible. A profile of the webview showed 70% of main-thread time inside event dispatch and JSON parsing, not in xterm.js rendering at all.

## Cause

Every stream delta from the agent — often a handful of bytes — was crossing the Tauri IPC boundary as its own `emit`, serialized to JSON and then parsed on the JS side, and each one triggered a React state update. A verbose build peaked at about 9,000 events per second.
