The renderer was never the bottleneck; the per-message overhead was, and it scaled with message *count*, so short chatty lines were far worse than one large blob.

## Fix and its limits

The supervisor now appends into a per-run ring buffer and flushes on a 16ms tick or at 64KB, whichever comes first, as one binary frame. Same build: ~60 events/s, typing latency back under 20ms.

Backpressure is part of the fix, not a separate feature. Agents can emit unbounded output (a test suite in a loop, a `yes`-shaped bug), and a buffer that only grows moves the crash from the UI thread to the allocator. Above 2MB unflushed we drop from the head and splice in `[… N lines elided]`. Users do see that marker occasionally and it is intentional; the full stream is still on disk in the run transcript.

We wanted a shared-memory ring instead of copying through IPC, and dropped it: WebView2 on Windows gives no usable shm path from the webview, and a platform-specific fast path was not worth maintaining twice.

pages.title: Cancelling a run left orphaned compilers alive because the signal went to the agent process, not its process group
pages.body:
## Symptom

After pressing Cancel the pane closed cleanly, but `esbuild` and `tsc --watch` kept a core busy, and port 3000 stayed bound so the user's next `pnpm dev` failed. Reproducible whenever the agent had started anything through an npm script.

## Cause

Spawn used a plain `Command::spawn` and cancel sent a signal to that one pid. Agent CLIs shell out constantly, and `npm run` forks a shell that forks the real tool, so the descendants were never signalled — they got reparented to init and carried on. Nothing in the code was wrong locally; the mistake was treating a run as one process rather than a tree.

## Fix

On Unix the child is put in its own session (`setsid`) and cancellation is `killpg` against the negated pgid. On Windows there are no process groups worth using, so the run is created inside a Job Object with `JOB_OBJECT_LIMIT_KILL_ON_JOB_CLOSE`, which kills the tree when the handle drops.

The escalation ladder matters and is easy to get wrong in the other direction: SIGINT, wait 2s, SIGTERM, wait 3s, SIGKILL. We started with SIGKILL immediately because it is simple, and lost the tail of every cancelled run — the agent CLI flushes its transcript and its final usage block on SIGINT, so killing outright cost us the last 200-400 tokens of context *and* the cost record for that turn, which then never appeared in the ledger ([[agents-cost-ledger-per-turn]]).

Freezing a run rather than ending it is a different path entirely — see [[agents-suspend-on-system-sleep]].

pages.title: On system sleep a run is frozen with SIGSTOP and resumed from the last message boundary, not restarted
pages.body:
## The constraint we could not change

When the machine sleeps, the streaming HTTP response dies. The provider has already generated — and already billed — whatever tokens were produced before the socket dropped. So "do nothing and let it fail" is not free: the user pays for a turn they never received.

## Options

*Keep the machine awake for the duration.* Rejected: holding an `IOPMAssertion` (or `SetThreadExecutionState` on Windows) for a 20-minute agent run drains a laptop that the user deliberately closed. Users close the lid because they mean it.

*Cancel and rerun on wake.* Rejected on cost and on safety. Cost was $0.30-$1.20 per interrupted run in our sample, but the real problem is that an agent halfway through a refactor has already written files; rerunning from the top makes it re-apply edits against a tree that is no longer clean, which is worse than losing the money.

## What we do

`NSWorkspaceWillSleepNotification` / `WM_POWERBROADCAST` triggers a SIGSTOP to the run's process group (same group machinery as [[agents-cancel-signal-escalation]]) and marks the run `suspended`. On wake we SIGCONT and give the agent's own transport 90s to reconnect. If the socket is genuinely dead, we resume from the **last complete assistant message**, never mid-message — a partial message replayed as context makes the model continue a sentence it does not remember starting, and in testing that produced duplicated tool calls.

Past 90s the run is marked `interrupted` and the pane offers Resume as a user action. We do not auto-resume after that, because by then the working tree may have been touched by the human.

pages.title: Spend is written per assistant turn as integer micro-dollars, so cancelled and retried runs still total correctly
pages.body:
## Shape

`agent_turn_cost(run_id, turn_ix, model, input, output, cache_write, cache_read, usd_micros, recorded_at)`, one row appended per assistant turn, never updated.

## Why per turn and append-only

The first version kept one row per run and updated it as the run progressed. Runs are not tidy: they get cancelled, suspended, resumed on another day, and retried. Every one of those is a mutation, and mutations are what we lost. A force-quit during a WAL checkpoint reliably dropped the last `UPDATE` while keeping the row, so a 40-minute run reported the cost of its first two minutes. Append-only rows mean a crash loses at most the turn in flight, and a cancelled run keeps everything it already spent — which is what the user was actually billed.

`turn_ix` exists so a resumed run does not double-count: the resume path knows the highest index already recorded.

## Two details that look arbitrary

Money is `INTEGER` micro-dollars. With `REAL` the monthly rollup accumulated drift on the order of $10^-9 per row, which is harmless until it renders as `$41.2300000000004` in the UI, which we shipped once.

Prices live in a `model_price` table seeded at build and refreshed by the updater, not in code. Provider pricing changed three times during 2025 and users on an older build were computing yesterday's rates against today's invoice with no way to notice. See [[agents-cost-cache-token-undercount]] for what happens when the token *categories* are wrong rather than the prices.

pages.title: Панель расходов занижала сумму втрое: cache-токены складывались с обычным input и считались по базовой цене
pages.body:
## Симптом

За день приложение показывало $4.10, счёт провайдера за тот же день — $12.80. Расхождение росло с длиной сессий: короткие запуски сходились почти точно, двухчасовые расходились в три-четыре раза.

## Причина

В usage-блоке ответа три отдельных счётчика входных токенов: `input_tokens`, `cache_creation_input_tokens` и `cache_read_input_tokens`. Мы складывали все три в одно поле `input` и умножали на базовую входную цену. Но запись в кэш стоит дороже базовой ставки, а чтение — заметно дешевле, и в длинной агентской сессии с большим системным промптом и растущим транскриптом почти весь объём уходит именно в эти две категории, а не в обычный input. Итог: доминирующая (и самая дорогая) часть счёта считалась по неправильному тарифу.

Вторая ошибка нашлась там же. Usage приходит дважды: `message_start` отдаёт предварительный блок с `output_tokens: 1`, `message_delta` — финальный. Мы суммировали оба, что добавляло лишний токен на каждый ход. На фоне первой ошибки это было незаметно, но при сверке мешало.

## Что сделали

Три счётчика хранятся отдельными колонками (схема в [[agents-cost-ledger-per-turn]]), тариф берётся по категории. За ход берётся **последний** usage, а не сумма. Миграция 0031 пересчитала историю по сохранённым счётчикам — они писались корректно, ломалась только арифметика, поэтому пересчёт был возможен без обращения к провайдеру.

Проверка: суточная сумма расходится со счётом не более чем на 1.5%, остаток — округление на стороне провайдера.

pages.title: The orchestrator retries a failed turn itself, up to 3 times with exponential backoff, by resending the transcript
pages.body:
## Why the orchestrator owns retries

Long runs die from short outages. Our failure sample over three weeks: 61% HTTP 529 overloaded, 22% TLS resets and DNS failures on café/hotel wifi, the rest genuine 4xx. Almost all of them clear within 30 seconds. Losing a 20-minute run — and its already-paid context — to a two-second network hiccup was the single loudest complaint about the agent panes.

The alternative was to let the agent CLI handle it, and the vendored CLI at 0.14 simply exited non-zero after one failed attempt with no backoff of its own. We are the layer that knows the run is worth saving, so we do it.

## Mechanics

`orchestrator/retry.ts` wraps the whole turn. On a non-zero exit or a stream error it waits 1s, 4s, 16s with ±25% jitter and re-sends the accumulated transcript as a fresh request, so the model resumes with full context. Three attempts, then the run is marked `failed`.

Not retried: exit code 2 (the user cancelled), and 401/403, which will not fix themselves and just delay the credentials prompt by 21 seconds.

The pane shows a subdued "reconnecting" line rather than an error, because from the user's point of view nothing has actually gone wrong yet.

## Known cost

A retried turn is billed twice — the provider charges for the partial generation we discarded. At current prices that is a few cents against a lost 20-minute run, so we take it silently rather than asking.

pages.title: Retries moved down into the HTTP client; replaying a transcript re-ran tool calls that had already executed
pages.body:
## The incident

A user's run created two identical commits ninety seconds apart. Three more reports followed, and one where a build directory was removed twice — harmless only by luck. All four runs had hit a stream error mid-turn.

Cause: resending the transcript is not idempotent once a `tool_use` block has been emitted **and executed**. The stream dies after the agent has run `git commit`, the retry replays context that ends before that block, and the model — correctly, given what it can see — issues the commit again. The old retry loop had no way to know which side effects had already landed, because side effects happen in the sandbox, not in the request.

## New rule

Retry only where no side effect can have occurred yet:

- connection failures before the first response byte
- 429/529 carrying `Retry-After`

That is a property of the transport, so it lives in the transport: `reqwest-middleware` with 3 attempts, honouring `Retry-After` up to 60s, capped at 8 retries per run in total.

Anything that fails *after* the first content block bubbles up. The turn is marked failed, the pane shows what the agent had done so far plus a Resume button, and the human decides. This is strictly worse ergonomics on bad wifi and we accepted that: an interrupted run is recoverable, a duplicated destructive command is not.

## What we did not build

Idempotency keys on tool execution, which would let us replay safely. It requires every tool to declare itself replayable, including shell commands, and there is no honest way to declare `rm -rf` replayable.

pages.title: Closing a pane detaches the run rather than killing it; the process survives 10 idle minutes and the transcript is on disk
pages.body:
## Getting a run back

Runs are owned by the supervisor process, keyed by `run_id`, and the webview is only a viewer. Closing a pane (⌘W included) detaches — the agent keeps working.

1. `zenith agents ls --detached` lists run id, pane title, age, and the last transcript line.
2. Command palette → "Reattach agent run", or `zenith agents attach <run-id>`, opens a new pane bound to the existing run and replays the tail of the transcript into it.
3. To actually stop one: `zenith agents cancel <run-id>` (full teardown path in [[agents-cancel-signal-escalation]]).

If the app itself crashed, the supervisor usually did not — it is a separate process, and reattaching works after the window comes back. If the supervisor died too, the run is gone but the transcript is not:

- macOS: `~/Library/Application Support/zenith/runs/<run-id>/transcript.jsonl`
- Linux: `~/.local/share/zenith/runs/<run-id>/`

Writes are appended and fsynced in 250ms batches, so a hard power loss costs at most a quarter second of output. Per-run cost rows are in SQLite independently and survive regardless.

## Why 10 minutes

Detached runs were originally kept until the app exited, on the theory that a background agent is exactly what you want. One tester accumulated 31 detached runs and 14GB of worktrees over a week without noticing, because nothing in the UI showed them. Now a detached run is reaped 600s after its last output — long enough to survive a mis-click and a window reload, short enough that forgetting about one is not expensive. Emitting output resets the timer, so a working agent is never reaped mid-thought.

pages.title: Запросы на подтверждение от всех агентов идут через один FIFO-брокер, а не всплывают в каждой панели
pages.body:
## Зачем брокер

При четырёх параллельных агентах модалки подтверждения всплывали независимо и дрались за фокус. Наблюдаемое поведение: диалог появлялся под курсором, пользователь бил Enter по мышечной памяти — и разрешал команду не того агента. В одном из отчётов так подтвердили `rm -rf` из панели, на которую человек в этот момент даже не смотрел.

Сама возможность спутать здесь важнее вероятности: подтверждение — единственное место, где человек берёт на себя ответственность за действие агента, и оно обязано быть однозначным.

## Как устроено

Очередь FIFO живёт в супервизоре, а не в UI, поэтому переживает перезагрузку окна. Одновременно показывается ровно один диалог: заголовок панели, рабочая директория, команда или диff целиком. Остальные панели показывают бейдж «ждёт подтверждения» и продолжают стримить то, что успели.

Таймаут 120 секунд трактуется как отказ. Это не про безопасность, а про деньги: провайдерская сессия висит открытой, пока агент ждёт ответа на tool call, и забытый диалог тихо жжёт время подписки.

## Автоправила

Правила авторазрешения хранятся per-workspace и матчатся **префиксом команды**, не регулярным выражением. Регэкспы обсуждались и были отклонены: `git .*` пишется на автомате и разрешает `git push --force` вместе со всем остальным. Префикс скучнее и его труднее случайно сделать слишком широким.

Очерёдность спавна панелей — в [[agents-pane-spawn-contract]].

pages.title: Agent processes get a rebuilt environment from an allowlist — inherited shell secrets were ending up in transcripts
pages.body:
## How we found it

A support bundle contained an `AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY` in plaintext inside a run transcript. The agent had not done anything unusual: a test failed, the harness printed the environment as part of its failure output, that output was captured as tool result, and the tool result went back to the provider as context. The key was in the transcript, in our crash bundle, and in the model's context window.

The general shape: anything in the agent's environment is one `printenv`, one verbose CI script, or one failing test away from being uploaded. Inheriting the launching shell's environment — which on a developer's machine is where every token lives — was the actual mistake.

## What we do

The environment is constructed, not inherited. Allowlist: `PATH`, `HOME`, `SHELL`, `LANG`, `LC_*`, `TERM`, `TZ`, `TMPDIR`, proxy variables, plus a per-workspace list the user adds explicitly in settings. Everything else is dropped. Agent credentials are injected by the supervisor into the transport, not exposed as a variable the agent process can read.

## Rejected

*Denylist of secret-looking names.* Pattern matching on `*_KEY`, `*_TOKEN`, `*_SECRET` catches the obvious ones and misses `MY_COMPANY_CREDS` or `NPM_CONFIG_//registry.npmjs.org/:_authToken`. A miss is a leak, so the default must be deny.

*Redacting secrets from output after the fact.* We cannot redact values we never passed and therefore never knew.

## Accepted risk

`SSH_AUTH_SOCK` is forwarded on purpose — agents push branches, and taking it away breaks the main workflow. An agent can use the agent socket to sign, but cannot read the private key. Documented in the threat model as accepted.

pages.title: Sync started with last-writer-wins per field and it silently ate half of a two-machine edit
pages.body:
## What we shipped first

The first sync engine treated a workspace document as a flat map of fields and resolved every collision with last-writer-wins on `updated_at`. Each field carried its own timestamp, so in theory two machines editing different fields never collided. The appeal was size: the wire payload was a map of `field -> (value, ts)` and the merge was thirty lines in `crates/sync/src/merge.rs`.

## Why it failed in practice

The model is wrong for anything with internal structure. A workspace's pane tree is not a field — it is a tree whose nodes reference each other. When a user split a pane on the laptop and renamed the parent tab on the desktop, LWW picked one whole `layout` blob and dropped the other. The user saw a rename that "undid" a split they had made minutes earlier, with no error and nothing in the log.

We also learned that field granularity does not save you: making the tree finer-grained (per node) produced dangling child references, because LWW has no notion of an invariant spanning two fields. A delete on machine A and a child-insert on machine B under the same parent produced an orphan node that crashed the layout restorer on next launch.

## The escape hatch we relied on

For eight months the mitigation was that sync only ran while exactly one machine was awake — the daemon backed off if it saw a heartbeat under 90s from another device. That made the bug rare enough to look like a ghost, which is why it stayed open so long.

pages.title: Workspace layout moved to an RGA-style CRDT so concurrent pane edits both survive
pages.body:
## The change

The pane tree is now a replicated structure rather than a versioned blob. Each node gets a stable `NodeId` = (device_uuid, lamport_counter), children are ordered by an RGA sequence, and deletion is a tombstone rather than a removal. Merging two states is a set union plus tombstone application, which is commutative and idempotent — so replay order and duplicate delivery stop mattering. Non-structural leaves (tab title, cwd, font scale) keep a register with a deterministic tiebreak: higher Lamport wins, device UUID breaks ties. That part is still effectively last-writer-wins, deliberately, because a title has no invariant to violate.

## Why not a library

We evaluated `yrs` (the Rust Yjs port) and `automerge` 0.5. Both are correct and both were rejected on size and shape. Automerge's document overhead measured 340 KB for a 12-pane workspace against 4 KB for the hand-rolled encoding, because it retains full change history for a document that nobody ever asks to time-travel. `yrs` was closer, but its awareness/transaction model assumes a live socket, and Zenith syncs over an object store with 30-second polling, not a persistent connection. We took the ~600 lines of RGA and own it.

## The cost we accepted

Tombstones never expire while any device is more than 30 days behind. A workspace that gets heavy pane churn grows monotonically; we compact only when every registered device has acknowledged a snapshot epoch. A device that is offline for a quarter therefore pins garbage for the whole account.

pages.title: A laptop with a 40-minute-fast RTC made its writes permanently win until we moved to hybrid logical clocks
pages.body:
## Symptom

One user reported that changes made on their desktop "never took" — settings edits reverted within a minute, every time, for two weeks. Every other device pair in the same account behaved fine.

## Cause

Their MacBook's RTC was 40 minutes ahead (a dead coin cell plus an NTP daemon the corporate MDM had disabled). Because our register tiebreak read `SystemTime::now()`, every value that laptop wrote carried a future timestamp and beat everything the desktop produced. There is no self-correction in wall-clock LWW: once a device is ahead, it wins forever, and the loss is silent.

## Fix and the constraint behind it

We moved to a hybrid logical clock (HLC) as described in Kulkarni et al. 2014: 48 bits of physical millis, 16 bits of logical counter. On receiving a remote timestamp, a device advances its own physical component to `max(local, remote)` — so a fast clock pulls the whole account forward once and then stops mattering, since ordering after that comes from the counter.

We explicitly did *not* clamp against server time. The sync backend is an S3-compatible bucket with no compute; there is no authoritative clock to ask, and adding one would have meant standing up a service purely for timestamps. The remaining guard is a sanity bound: a remote HLC more than 24h ahead of local physical time is rejected with `SkewTooLarge` and surfaced in the sync status pane, rather than being absorbed into the local clock. That bound is what stops a single corrupted device from dragging every device's clock into 2038.

pages.title: Chunk uploads write the manifest last, because a torn multi-object write is invisible to an object store
pages.body:
## The problem an object store creates

A sync push is several PUTs: N content chunks plus one manifest that names them. The bucket gives us per-object atomicity and nothing else — there is no transaction spanning objects. If the process dies, or the network drops, or the user closes the lid after chunk 3 of 7, the bucket is left in a state no reader can distinguish from a healthy one unless we impose an order.

## The ordering rule

Chunks are content-addressed (`blake3` of the plaintext, then encrypted), written to `chunks/<hash>`, and are immutable. The manifest at `manifests/<device>/<epoch>.json` is written **only after every chunk PUT has returned 200**. A reader that finds a manifest can therefore assume every chunk it references exists. A chunk with no manifest pointing at it is garbage, not data — it costs storage and is collected on the next full sweep, but it can never be read as a partial state.

This is why resume is cheap: the client re-lists `chunks/`, diffs against what the new manifest needs, and only uploads what is missing. A 900 MB workspace history interrupted at 80% re-uploads roughly 180 MB, not 900.

## Why not multipart upload

S3 multipart gives atomic completion for *one* object, which would have let us pack everything into a single blob. We rejected it because the same manifest has to work on backends that are not S3 — the self-hosted target is a WebDAV mount and Backblaze B2 via its native API, and multipart semantics differ across all three. Ordering constraints are portable; vendor atomicity is not.

pages.title: Scrollback deltas use content-defined chunking at 64 KB average, not fixed blocks
pages.body:
## Why fixed blocks lost

The first delta format cut the session scrollback into fixed 64 KB blocks and shipped changed blocks. It worked until scrollback got *prepended* to — which happens on every restore-and-continue, because we merge the persisted tail before the new output. A single byte inserted at the front shifted every block boundary and made a 40 MB scrollback fully dirty. Users on tethered connections saw the sync indicator spin for minutes after opening a saved session.

## What we use now

FastCDC (Xia et al., ATC 2016) with a 16 KB minimum, 64 KB normal and 256 KB maximum chunk size, gear-hash based. Boundaries follow content, so an insertion perturbs at most the two chunks around it. Measured on our own corpus of 200 recorded sessions, the median push after a restore dropped from 38 MB to 210 KB.

We deliberately do not compress before chunking — compression destroys the boundary stability that makes CDC work. Order is: chunk, then zstd level 3 per chunk, then encrypt per chunk with a key derived from the chunk hash. That last step is what makes chunks shareable across devices without the server learning anything, but it also means identical plaintext produces identical ciphertext, so the backend can see which chunks two devices have in common. We accepted that leak; the alternative is losing dedup entirely.

## Tuning note

The 64 KB average is not from a paper, it is from us: below 32 KB the manifest itself became the dominant cost for large histories (one 8 MB manifest for a 2 GB account), above 128 KB dedup on terminal output fell off a cliff because ANSI-heavy output has poor locality.

pages.title: Sync conflicts resolve silently and never prompt the user, by design
pages.body:
## The rejected design

The original spec had a conflict dialog: when two devices disagreed, show both versions and let the user pick. We built it, ran it internally for six weeks, and removed it.

## Why it did not survive contact

The dialog fired an average of 11 times a week per person, and in every single logged case the user picked whichever option was on top. The reason is structural: the things that conflict in a terminal workspace are not things a person has an opinion about. Nobody wants to adjudicate whether the cwd of pane 3 is `~/src/zenith` or `~/src/zenith/crates`. The conflicts a user *would* care about — two different agent sessions writing to the same pane — turned out to be prevented upstream by pane ownership leases, not by merge.

A second problem killed it outright: the dialog blocked at a moment the user had no context for. Sync lands 30 seconds after a poll, so the prompt arrives detached from the action that caused it, often on the machine that did not make either edit.

## What we do instead

Merge is always automatic and always deterministic. Every non-trivial resolution writes a row to `sync_resolution_log` with both operand values, and the settings pane exposes the last 50 as a plain read-only list with a per-row "restore this value" button. Recovery is a user-initiated action after the fact rather than a modal before it. In 14 months the restore button has been pressed 40 times account-wide across roughly 900k automatic resolutions.

pages.title: The updater originally downloaded a full application package for every release
pages.body:
## How it worked

Every update was a complete signed archive: 78 MB on macOS (universal binary), 61 MB on Windows, 66 MB for the Linux AppImage. The updater fetched the whole thing to a temp dir, verified the signature over the complete file, and swapped the install directory. Simple, auditable, and the signature check covered every byte the user would run.

## Why we accepted the size at first

Two reasons, both real at the time. First, the Tauri updater plugin we were building on only understood whole-artifact replacement, and diverging from it meant owning the platform-specific install swap on three OSes. Second, the signature story is trivially correct: one artifact, one minisign signature, no way to assemble a binary that was never signed as a unit.

## What made it untenable

Release cadence. We moved from monthly to weekly, and the CDN bill went from $340/mo to $2,900/mo — 94% of it was users re-downloading bytes that had not changed between builds. Worse was the user-side effect: telemetry showed a long tail of installs on metered or slow links where the update never completed, because a 78 MB download with no resume would fail and restart from zero. 6.2% of active installs were more than four releases behind, and that cohort was almost entirely users on connections under 3 Mbps.

The decision to keep full packages was correct while releases were monthly. It stopped being correct the moment cadence changed, and the trigger was a cost line item, not an engineering complaint.

pages.title: Updates ship as bsdiff patches against the previous three releases, with a full package fallback
pages.body:
## The format

CI now emits, for release N, patches from N-1, N-2 and N-3 alongside the full archive. Patches are `bsdiff` 4.3 output wrapped in our own header (source hash, target hash, target size). Median macOS patch is 2.1 MB against 78 MB full — the binary is mostly unchanged Rust and the React bundle diffs well. A client more than three releases behind, or on a platform where patching failed, silently falls back to the full download.

## The signature rule that this forced

We sign the **target**, not the patch. The updater applies the patch to the on-disk binary, hashes the result, and verifies that hash against a minisign signature over the reconstructed artifact from the release manifest. Signing the patch instead would have been cheaper but is unsound: it only proves the diff came from us, not that the machine's source binary was the one we diffed against. A tampered installed binary plus a genuine patch produces a tampered result that a patch-signature scheme would happily accept.

## What bit us during rollout

bsdiff's memory use is roughly 17x the target size — patch *generation* on CI peaked at 1.4 GB and pushed the GitHub-hosted runner into swap, doubling release job time. Generation moved to a 8 GB self-hosted runner. Application on the client is cheap by comparison but still allocates the full target in memory, which is why we disable patching entirely on machines reporting under 512 MB free.

See [[sync-updater-signature-chain]] for what actually holds the key.

pages.title: Update signing uses an offline minisign root that certifies a rotating release key
pages.body:
## Structure

There are two keys. The **root** is a minisign Ed25519 keypair whose secret half exists only on an air-gapped machine and on two paper backups in separate physical locations. It signs nothing but key certificates. The **release key** is generated quarterly, its public half is signed by the root, and the resulting certificate ships inside every build. CI holds only the release secret, in the GitHub Actions secret store.

A client verifies in two steps: check the release-key certificate against the root public key that was compiled into the running binary, then check the artifact signature against the certified release key. The root public key is a `const` in `crates/updater/src/keys.rs` — deliberately not fetched, not configurable, not overridable by settings.

## Why rotation matters more than key strength

The threat we designed for is not someone breaking Ed25519, it is CI compromise. A leaked release key is survivable: revoke it, issue a new certificate from the root, and clients reject the old key after its `not_after` date. A leaked root key means every install must be replaced by hand, which for a desktop app means it is over. Splitting them turns a plausible incident into a bad week.

## The constraint we cannot get around

Certificate expiry creates a floor on update laziness. A build older than one rotation period cannot verify the current release key, because its embedded root is fine but the certificate chain assumes overlapping validity windows. We overlap certificates by two quarters for this reason. Anything older than ~6 months must be reinstalled manually, and the updater says so explicitly instead of failing with a signature error.

pages.title: Откат обновления работает через второй слот установки, а не через переустановку старой версии
pages.body:
## Как устроено

Приложение ставится в два слота: `app/current` и `app/previous`. Обновление распаковывается в неактивный слот, и только после успешной проверки подписи и первого запуска символическая ссылка `app/active` переключается. Старый слот остаётся нетронутым до следующего обновления, то есть на диске всегда лежит ровно одна предыдущая версия — примерно 80 МБ постоянного оверхеда, на который мы сознательно пошли.

## Почему не откатываемся скачиванием

Очевидный вариант — при сбое просто скачать предыдущий релиз с CDN. Мы его отвергли по двум причинам. Первая: откат нужен чаще всего именно тогда, когда что-то сломано настолько, что сеть недоступна или сам апдейтер не стартует. Вторая: мы удаляем артефакты старше 90 дней из бакета, чтобы не платить за хранение всей истории сборок, и пользователь на версии полугодовой давности откатиться было бы некуда.

## Триггер отката

Переключение слота откладывается до тех пор, пока новый бинарник не отчитается о здоровье: процесс должен прожить 20 секунд и записать маркер `healthy` в `state/boot.json`. Три подряд неудачных старта (счётчик в том же файле) означают автоматический возврат на `previous` и всплывающее уведомление. Именно эта схема поймала регрессию 0.34.1, где падал инициализатор WebGL-рендерера на драйверах Intel Iris — упало примерно 4% ставящихся, но откат сработал молча, и в поддержку пришло всего два обращения.

pages.title: Staged rollout buckets by a hash of the install UUID, so a device stays in the same cohort across releases
pages.body:
## How to ship a staged release

The release manifest carries a `rollout` field with a percentage. The client computes `blake3(install_uuid || channel)[0..4]` as a u32, maps it to 0-9999, and takes the update only if that number is below `rollout * 100`. No server-side targeting; the manifest is a static file on the CDN and every client decides for itself.

Ramp it by editing the manifest and re-uploading:

```
scripts/rollout.sh 0.36.0 --to 5     # 5%
scripts/rollout.sh 0.36.0 --to 25
scripts/rollout.sh 0.36.0 --to 100
```

Hold at each step until the crash-free-session rate over the last 2h is within 0.3pp of the previous release. That number comes from telemetry, so it is only meaningful once ~2,000 sessions have landed on the new build, which at 5% takes roughly six hours.

## The property that matters

The hash does **not** include the version. That is deliberate: a device in the first 5% is in the first 5% for every release. It means our early cohort is a stable population we can reason about, and it means a user who hits an early-release bug once is not statistically more likely than anyone else to hit the next one — they are *guaranteed* to be exposed again. We considered mixing the version into the hash to spread that risk and rejected it, because a stable cohort makes "did this regression come from the new build or from that population" answerable at all. Internal and opt-in beta installs are hashed into bucket 0 by forcing `install_uuid` into a reserved range at first run.

## Aborting

Setting `rollout` to 0 stops new installs but does not recall the ones already updated — recall is [[sync-updater-rollback-slot]], and it only triggers on health failure, never on a manifest edit.

pages.title: Deleted workspaces came back because tombstones were pruned before a slow device had seen them
pages.body:
## Symptom

Support ticket, then four more in a fortnight: a user deletes a workspace, it stays gone for days, then reappears — sometimes weeks later, always after the user had used a machine they rarely open.

## Cause

Compaction dropped tombstones older than 30 days on the assumption that every device would have synced by then. It is a fine assumption for phones and a bad one for a work laptop that gets opened once a quarter. The stale device still held the workspace as live, saw no tombstone (it had been compacted away), and its state union re-introduced the record. From the CRDT's point of view nothing went wrong — an absent tombstone is indistinguishable from a delete that never happened. This is the classic resurrection failure and our 30-day window was a guess, not a bound.

## Fix

Compaction is now gated on acknowledgement rather than age. Each device writes `acks/<device>.json` with the highest epoch it has fully merged; tombstones are only pruned below `min(ack)` across devices that have been seen in the last 180 days. Devices silent for more than 180 days are dropped from the quorum entirely and are forced into a full-resync on their next connection — they discard local state and rebuild from the current snapshot, which loses any offline edits they were holding.

That last part is a real data-loss path and we chose it knowingly. The alternative is unbounded tombstone retention, and we already had one account at 61 MB of tombstones for 3 MB of live data because of a single decommissioned machine that never formally deregistered.

pages.title: Sync encryption keys derive from a passphrase via Argon2id, and losing it is unrecoverable by design
pages.body:
## Derivation

The user's sync passphrase goes through Argon2id (m=64 MiB, t=3, p=4, 32-byte output) with a per-account random salt stored in the bucket alongside the manifests. The result is a root key; per-chunk keys are HKDF-SHA256 expansions keyed by the chunk's plaintext blake3 hash, which is what gives us convergent encryption and therefore cross-device dedup. Content is sealed with XChaCha20-Poly1305, nonce = first 24 bytes of the chunk hash, safe because the key is unique per chunk content.

## Why the parameters are what they are

64 MiB was chosen against the low end of our hardware, not the high end. The passphrase is entered on every fresh device setup, and on a 2017 dual-core ThinkPad the derivation takes 900 ms at these settings; at 256 MiB it took 3.4 s and testers read that as a hang. We did not go below 64 MiB because Argon2id's resistance argument weakens sharply and the threat here is an offline attack against a bucket that may be a third-party S3 the user does not control.

## No recovery, and what that costs us

There is no escrow, no server-held wrapping key, no reset. If the passphrase is lost, every chunk in the bucket is permanently opaque — support cannot help, and the honest answer in the ticket is "delete the bucket and start over." We keep it this way because the self-hosted story is the reason people choose Zenith over the alternatives, and any recovery mechanism that works without the passphrase also works for whoever holds the bucket. The setup flow forces the user to retype the passphrase after a 60-second delay to make the loss concrete before it happens.

pages.title: The sync poller backs off to 15 minutes on idle because S3 LIST requests, not bandwidth, dominated cost
pages.body:
## What we found

A month after launching sync on the hosted backend, the storage bill came in at $1,180 against an expected ~$200. Egress was 8% of it. The rest was request cost: every client issued a LIST on `manifests/` every 30 seconds, awake or not, and LIST is billed at roughly 10x the rate of GET. 14,000 active installs times 2,880 LISTs/day is 40M requests a day for a workspace most of which had not changed since the previous week.

## Why it was not obvious

Because in dev it costs nothing. We tested against MinIO on a laptop where a LIST is free and instant, so the polling interval was tuned purely for perceived latency and nobody looked at the shape of the traffic until the invoice arrived. This is the second time an S3-semantics difference bit us — see [[sync-partial-upload-manifest-last]] for the other one.

## Current behaviour

Polling is 30 s while any pane has had input in the last 2 minutes, then steps 30 s → 2 min → 15 min. It resets to 30 s on local input, on window focus, and on resume from sleep. Push is unaffected — a local change uploads immediately, it never waits for a poll tick.

The visible cost is that a change made on machine A can take up to 15 minutes to appear on an idle machine B. We tried to close that with an SNS/websocket wake channel and dropped it: it required a server component, which breaks the bring-your-own-bucket setup that a third of paying users are on. Latency on idle machines was judged the cheaper loss.

pages.title: Revoking a device rotates the account key but cannot un-read what that device already pulled
pages.body:
## Procedure

From Settings → Sync → Devices, remove the device. Behind that button:

1. The device UUID is added to `revoked.json` in the bucket and its `acks/` entry is deleted, dropping it from the compaction quorum immediately.
2. The user is prompted for a new passphrase; a fresh salt is written and the root key is re-derived.
3. Every live chunk is re-encrypted under the new key and written to `chunks-v<n+1>/`, then the old prefix is deleted. For a 2 GB account on a 50 Mbit uplink this takes about 25 minutes and must run on a machine that already holds the current passphrase.
4. Remaining devices detect the salt change on their next poll and prompt for the new passphrase. They cannot proceed until the user enters it — there is no silent handoff, because a silent handoff would mean the old key material could unwrap the new one.

## What revocation does not do

It does not retroactively protect anything the revoked device already downloaded and decrypted, which for a normally-used laptop is the entire workspace history. Revocation limits future access; it is not a remote wipe. The settings copy says exactly this, deliberately, because the earlier wording ("remove access") produced support tickets from users who assumed a stolen laptop's local `.zenith/` cache had been neutralised.

## The gap we know about

If the revoked device is online during step 3 and still holds the old passphrase, it can read the pre-rotation chunks until deletion finishes. We do not have a way to close this without server-side auth, which the bring-your-own-bucket deployment does not have. Advise users to remove local data on the device physically when it is available.

pages.title: Themes compile to CSS custom properties at load, not to a JS theme object passed through React context
pages.body:
## Why not context

The first theming implementation kept the active theme as a plain object in a `ThemeProvider` and every styled component read it through `useContext`. Switching theme re-rendered the whole tree, including the pane grid. On a 4-pane workspace that cost 180-240ms and xterm.js canvases got remounted because their wrapper identity changed. Users perceived theme switching as a visible flash.

We now parse the theme file once, emit ~90 `--zn-*` custom properties into a single `<style id="zn-theme">` element in the document head, and swap that element's text content on change. React never re-renders; the browser repaints. Measured 8-14ms on the same workspace.

## The part that leaks

xterm.js does not read CSS variables — its `ITheme` wants literal color strings. So the terminal is the one consumer that still needs a JS object. `applyTheme()` resolves the sixteen ANSI slots plus background/foreground/cursor via `getComputedStyle(document.documentElement)` after the style element is swapped, then calls `term.options.theme = {...}` on every open terminal. That resolve step must happen in a `requestAnimationFrame` callback; reading computed style in the same tick as the swap returns the previous values in WebKit (reproduced on macOS 14, not on Linux WebKitGTK).

## Constraint

Plugin-supplied themes therefore may only declare colors, never selectors — an arbitrary CSS blob would be un-resolvable into the xterm bridge and would let a plugin restyle the trust prompts.

pages.title: Settings moved from JSON to TOML because comments survived round-trips and JSON5 parsers disagreed
pages.body:
## The failure JSON caused

The original `settings.json` was rewritten in full whenever the settings UI saved. Anything a user had hand-edited — ordering, grouping, and especially the comments people wrote next to keybindings — was destroyed. We tried JSON5 to at least allow comments, but the Rust side (`json5` crate) and the TS side (`json5` npm) disagreed on trailing commas inside nested arrays, so a file the UI wrote could fail to load in the core.

## What we chose

`settings.toml`, edited through `toml_edit` on the Rust side. `toml_edit` is a format-preserving parser: it holds the document as a tree of spans, so setting one value rewrites exactly those bytes and leaves whitespace and comments untouched. The frontend no longer serializes settings at all — it sends a typed patch (`{path: ["terminal","fontSize"], value: 13}`) over IPC and the core applies it.

## Costs we accepted

- TOML has no null. Clearing an override means removing the key, so the patch protocol needed an explicit `Unset` variant rather than `value: null`.
- Deeply nested maps read badly in TOML. We flattened `keybindings` from a nested object into an array of tables, which changed the migration path — `migrations/003_json_to_toml.rs` has to reshape, not just transcode.
- Arrays of mixed types are rejected by the spec, which caught two bugs in the old keybinding format that JSON had silently allowed.

pages.title: Plugins run as Node subprocesses over JSON-RPC; the WASM component-model sandbox was abandoned mid-implementation
pages.body:
## What we tried first

The plugin API was specced against the WebAssembly component model with `wasmtime` 21 and WIT bindings. The appeal was real isolation: no filesystem, no network, deterministic resource limits, and a host that could kill a runaway plugin in microseconds.

It died on the ecosystem. Plugin authors write TypeScript. The only credible TS-to-WASM path was Javy/QuickJS, which gave us a 6-8MB artifact per plugin, no async host calls without a manual reactor loop, and no debugger story at all. Two of the three design-partner authors gave up during the pilot; the third shipped a plugin that took 400ms to cold-start because QuickJS had to re-parse its bundle on every activation.

## Current design

Each plugin is a Node process spawned with `--disallow-code-generation-from-strings`, talking newline-delimited JSON-RPC over stdio. Capability enforcement is in the host: the plugin declares `permissions` in its manifest and the host refuses RPC methods outside that set. Filesystem access is mediated — the plugin never gets a path, it gets an opaque handle the host resolves.

## What we knowingly gave up

A malicious plugin can still read the user's home directory directly through Node's `fs`, because the process is not OS-sandboxed. We accepted this and made it explicit in the install prompt rather than pretending the permission list is a security boundary. Revisiting is blocked on a per-platform sandbox (seatbelt / bubblewrap / AppContainer), tracked separately — see [[platform-plugin-process-sandbox]].

pages.title: Plugin subprocesses are now confined by OS sandboxes (seatbelt, bubblewrap, AppContainer), reversing the "permissions are advisory" stance
pages.body:
## Why we came back to it

A plugin published to the community registry (`zenith-git-status`, v0.4.1) shipped a postinstall-equivalent in its activation path that read `~/.ssh/id_ed25519` and posted it to a pastebin. It was caught by a user, not by us. The manifest declared only `terminal:read`. The old position — that the permission list is documentation, not a boundary — became untenable the moment we had a registry.

## What we did instead of returning to WASM

WASM was still rejected for the reasons in the superseded page; nothing about the tooling improved. Instead the host now wraps the Node spawn in a per-OS confinement:

- **macOS**: `sandbox-exec` with a generated seatbelt profile. Deprecated since 10.14 and Apple has never removed it; we accept the risk and have a fallback that refuses to spawn if the profile fails to compile.
- **Linux**: `bubblewrap` when present, otherwise a `seccomp` filter applied in a pre-exec hook. Flatpak builds get bwrap for free.
- **Windows**: AppContainer via `CreateProcessAsUser` with a low-integrity token. Named-pipe stdio had to replace anonymous pipes because AppContainer processes cannot inherit ordinary handles.

## The cost nobody predicted

Cold start went from 90ms to 210-260ms on macOS because seatbelt profile compilation is not cached by the OS. We cache the compiled profile per plugin-version under `~/Library/Caches/dev.zenith/sandbox/` and only recompile when the manifest hash changes.

pages.title: Telemetry is opt-in with no first-run prompt; the opt-out design was reversed after the EU launch review
pages.body:
## What shipped in 0.3

Telemetry defaulted to on. A dismissible banner in the corner said "anonymous usage data is being collected" with a link to settings. Legal signed off on it for the US. The counter-argument at the time — that opt-out gets you 20x the sample and the data is genuinely anonymous — carried the decision.

## Why it did not survive

The pre-launch review for the EU distribution flagged two things. First, GDPR consent must be affirmative and pre-ticked boxes do not count (Planet49, C-673/17); a banner that collects unless dismissed is exactly the pre-ticked box. Second — and this was the one we had not thought about — our "anonymous" event payload included the workspace name and the shell command that started a pane, which is personal data the moment anyone names a workspace after a client.

## Current behaviour

Nothing is sent before the user turns it on in Settings → Privacy. There is no first-run modal at all: the modal-with-two-buttons pattern was rejected because it trains people to click through, and because the conversion rate on such modals (~8% genuine reads in the vendor's own study) is not worth the launch friction. Discovery is a one-line entry in the settings page and a mention in the release notes.

Sample size fell from ~62% of installs to 4.1%. We compensate by treating telemetry as directional only — no A/B decisions are made on it, and crash reporting is a separate consent toggle described in [[platform-crash-reports-separate-consent]].

pages.title: Crash reports have their own consent toggle and a separate scrubbing pipeline from usage telemetry
pages.body:
## Two systems that look like one

Usage telemetry and crash reporting share nothing but the word "telemetry" in casual speech. Usage events are structured, low-volume, and generated by our own code, so scrubbing is a matter of not putting sensitive fields in the struct. Crash reports are minidumps produced by `minidumper`/`crashpad` in the Rust core and unstructured stack traces from the webview — both contain whatever happened to be on the stack, which for a terminal emulator routinely includes shell history and a partially-typed password.

They therefore have separate consent flags (`privacy.usage_stats`, `privacy.crash_reports`) and a user can enable either without the other. Roughly 11% of consenting users enable crash reports only.

## What scrubbing actually does

For minidumps we ship with `MINIDUMP_TYPE = MiniDumpNormal | MiniDumpWithoutOptionalData`, which omits the full heap. This is the whole reason the reports are ~250KB instead of 40MB, and it is also why some use-after-free reports are unactionable — we cannot see the freed contents. That tradeoff was made deliberately.

For webview traces we regex-strip anything matching a path under `$HOME` and replace it with `~`, then drop any frame whose source URL is a plugin. Plugin frames were leaking plugin-local file paths that contained project names.

## What is not scrubbed

The crashing thread's register values. We could not find a way to redact them without making the reports useless, so the consent copy states plainly that a crash report may contain fragments of terminal content.

pages.title: Notarization stapling fails intermittently because notarytool returns before the ticket is published to Apple's CDN
pages.body:
## Symptom

About one release in four, `xcrun stapler staple Zenith.app` failed in CI with `Error 65 — could not find the ticket`, immediately after `xcrun notarytool submit --wait` had returned `status: Accepted`. Re-running the same stapler command by hand ten minutes later always worked. We initially blamed the runner's network.

## Cause

`notarytool --wait` returns when the submission's status flips to Accepted in the notary service's own database. The stapling ticket is fetched from a separate CDN endpoint (`api.apple-cloudkit.com`) and its propagation is asynchronous. There is no documented SLA; observed lag was 5s to just over 3 minutes, and it is worse for submissions accepted during Apple's US-morning peak. Nothing about this is in the notarytool docs — it was confirmed on the Apple developer forums and by watching the failure correlate with time of day.

## Fix

`scripts/release/staple.sh` now retries stapling with exponential backoff: 10 attempts, 5s initial delay, 1.6x factor, capped at 60s, total ceiling ~6 minutes. Anything past that fails the job loudly rather than shipping an unstapled bundle — an unstapled but notarized app still launches when the machine is online, so this failure is invisible in testing and only bites users who first launch offline.

The same retry wrapper is needed for the DMG, which must be stapled separately after the `.app` inside it is stapled and the DMG is rebuilt.

pages.title: The hardened runtime needs allow-jit for the WebView but must not get allow-unsigned-executable-memory
pages.body:
## The two entitlements people confuse

WKWebView's JavaScriptCore compiles JIT code, and under the hardened runtime that requires `com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit`. This entitlement permits `MAP_JIT` mappings, which are write-xor-execute: a page is either writable or executable, never both, and JSC flips them through `pthread_jit_write_protect_np`.

The entitlement that looks similar, `com.apple.security.cs.allow-unsigned-executable-memory`, disables code-signing enforcement on *all* executable pages in the process. It is strictly weaker security and it is not what the WebView needs. We had it in `entitlements.plist` for four months because an early Tauri template included it, and removing it changed nothing at runtime.

## What we actually ship

```xml
<key>com.apple.security.cs.allow-jit</key><true/>
<key>com.apple.security.cs.disable-library-validation</key><true/>
```

Library validation must be off because the plugin host loads Node native addons (`.node` files) that are signed with the plugin author's identity, not ours. Without it, `dlopen` fails with `code signature ... not valid for use in process`.

## Order matters

Sign inner binaries first (sidecar `zenith-core`, any `.dylib`, the Node runtime), then the `.app` bundle with `--options runtime --entitlements`. Signing the bundle first and then touching an inner binary invalidates the outer signature silently — `codesign --verify --deep --strict` catches it, plain `--verify` does not. CI runs the strict form.

pages.title: Windows signing moved from an EV hardware token to Azure Trusted Signing after the token blocked CI
pages.body:
## The problem with the token

The EV code-signing certificate lived on a SafeNet USB token that physically had to be plugged into a machine. That machine was a Windows box under a desk. Releases could not run on hosted GitHub runners, the token's PIN had to be entered by a human for the first sign of each session (SafeNet's "single logon" mode is a per-process cache, not persistent), and when the token was misplaced for six days in March we could not ship a security patch.

The self-hosted-runner workaround also meant our release machine was the only place with the private key and no HSM attestation of who used it.

## What replaced it

Azure Trusted Signing (formerly Azure Code Signing). The key never leaves Microsoft's HSM; CI authenticates with a federated OIDC token from GitHub Actions, so there is no long-lived secret in the repo either. `signtool` uses the `Azure.CodeSigning.Dlib` provider via `/dlib`.

## Things that surprised us

- Trusted Signing issues **short-lived certificates** (72 hours). Signatures stay valid only because they are RFC 3161 timestamped — timestamping is not optional here, it is load-bearing. A build signed without `/tr` starts failing SmartScreen three days later.
- Onboarding required a verified organisation with 3+ years of legal existence. A subsidiary we tried first was rejected.
- The identity validation is per-subscription, so the sandbox and production Azure subscriptions needed separate approvals, three weeks apart.
- Reputation did not carry over. SmartScreen treated the new publisher identity as unknown for roughly two weeks and ~4200 downloads.

pages.title: Linux builds are produced in a Debian 11 container to pin the glibc floor at 2.31
pages.body:
## The constraint

glibc is forward-compatible, not backward-compatible: a binary linked against 2.35 will not start on a system with 2.31, failing with `version GLIBC_2.34 not found`. Building on the CI runner's default image (Ubuntu 24.04, glibc 2.39) produced an AppImage that ran nowhere except recent distros. We got the report from a Debian 12 user, which has 2.36, so even that was too new.

## What we do

All Linux artifacts are built inside `debian:bullseye` (glibc 2.31) with a hand-installed newer Rust toolchain and Node 20 from nodesource. That floor was chosen to cover RHEL 9 (2.34), Debian 12 (2.36), and Ubuntu 22.04 (2.35) with margin, without going as far back as manylinux2014 (2.17), which cannot build webkit2gtk-4.1.

`webkit2gtk-4.1` versus `4.0` is the second axis and it is not something we can paper over: Ubuntu 22.04 ships 4.0, 24.04 ships 4.1, and the sonames differ. We build two `.deb` variants and pick in the download page by distro detection. The AppImage bundles neither — it declares webkit as an external requirement, because bundling GTK/webkit into an AppImage reliably breaks the system's input-method modules (ibus/fcitx stop working for CJK input).

## Check before shipping

`scripts/release/check-glibc.sh` runs `objdump -T` over every ELF in the bundle and fails if any symbol requires above 2.31. It caught a regression when a transitive dep started using `arc4random_buf` (glibc 2.36).

pages.title: Релизы собираются по git-тегу, а не по кнопке workflow_dispatch
pages.body:
## Что было

Сначала релизная сборка запускалась вручную через `workflow_dispatch` с полем ввода версии. Это дважды привело к тому, что опубликованный артефакт не соответствовал ни одному коммиту в истории: человек вводил `0.6.2`, но запускал workflow с ветки, где уже были смёржены посторонние коммиты. Восстановить, что именно попало в бинарь, оказалось невозможно — сборка не оставляла ссылки на SHA.

## Что сейчас

Единственный триггер релиза — push аннотированного тега `v*`. Пайплайн:

1. Проверяет, что `Cargo.toml`, `package.json` и `tauri.conf.json` содержат ровно ту версию, что в теге, иначе падает до сборки.
2. Собирает три платформы параллельно из одного и того же `github.sha`.
3. Пишет SHA и тег в `zenith --version` через `build.rs` (переменная `ZENITH_BUILD_SHA`).
4. Публикует draft-релиз; человек только нажимает Publish.

## Почему не semantic-release

Обсуждали автогенерацию версий из conventional commits. Отказались: у нас релизы завязаны на нотаризацию и на подпись, которые стоят ~25 минут и требуют ручного решения «идём или нет» после smoke-теста. Полностью автоматический выпуск означал бы, что случайный `feat:` в merge-коммите отправляет сборку в подпись. Компромисс — тег ставит человек, всё остальное автоматически.

## Побочный эффект

Перевыпуск той же версии невозможен без удаления тега. Это осознанно: удаление тега — заметное действие, в отличие от повторного нажатия кнопки.

pages.title: The updater verifies a minisign key baked into the binary, so key rotation needs a two-release bridge
pages.body:
## How verification works

Tauri's updater checks an Ed25519 (minisign format) signature over the downloaded archive against a public key compiled into the running application. This is deliberately independent of code signing: Apple/Microsoft signatures prove the bundle came from us at install time, but the updater must verify the *payload* before it ever writes it to disk, on a machine where OS-level verification happens too late.

The consequence people miss: the key that validates an update lives in the **old** binary. If we rotate the private key, every already-installed copy is checking against the previous public key and will reject everything we sign afterwards. There is no server-side fix; those installs are stranded and need a manual reinstall.

## The bridge procedure

Rotation takes two releases:

1. Release N is signed with the **old** key and its embedded pubkey list contains **both** old and new. Tauri's updater accepts a signature matching any key in the list (we patched this in via `updater.pubkey` accepting a newline-separated set — upstream only supports one, so `crates/updater/src/verify.rs` does the check itself).
2. Wait until adoption of N exceeds ~95% — measured off the update-check endpoint's User-Agent version, not telemetry, since telemetry is opt-in.
3. Release N+1 is signed with the new key only.

Anyone who never installed N is stranded at that point, which is why step 2 waits on real numbers rather than a fixed calendar delay. During the 0.5 rotation the tail took 11 weeks.

## Key storage

The private key is a GitHub environment secret on `production`, requiring a second approver to run the release job.

pages.title: The plugin API is versioned by capability strings, not by a single semver number on the host
pages.body:
## Why a host version did not work

The first design had plugins declare `"zenithApi": "^1.2.0"` and the host refuse to load anything outside range. Within two months we had a situation where a plugin needed one method added in 1.4 and nothing else, but users on 1.3 got a hard refusal and a support ticket. Bumping minor versions for every added method also meant the range in every manifest went stale immediately, so authors started writing `">=1.0.0"` and the check became decoration.

## Capability strings

A manifest now declares what it uses:

```json
"requires": ["pane.split@1", "terminal.write@1", "statusbar.item@2"]
```

The host publishes the set it implements. Load fails only if a required capability is absent, and the error names exactly which one — which turned a vague "incompatible plugin" into an actionable message. Adding a method is invisible to existing plugins; changing a method's shape means publishing `@2` and keeping `@1` for at least two minor releases.

## The cost

We now carry old capability implementations. `pane.split@1` has an argument order that nobody would design today and it will exist until we drop it in a major. We keep a deprecation table in `docs/plugin-api/capabilities.md` with the release each `@1` is scheduled to be removed, and the host logs a warning at load so authors see it in development rather than at removal.

This is orthogonal to how plugins are *isolated* — see [[platform-plugin-process-sandbox]] for that.

pages.title: Machine-local settings are excluded from sync by an explicit denylist, not by a naming convention
pages.body:
## What broke

After settings sync shipped, users with a laptop and a desktop reported the font size flipping between two values every few minutes, and one user's shell path was set to a Homebrew path that did not exist on their Linux machine, leaving every new pane failing to spawn.

## Cause

Sync originally pushed the whole `settings.toml` document. Some keys are inherently machine-local: `terminal.fontSize` (different DPI), `terminal.shell` (different paths), `window.bounds`, `gpu.rendererOverride`. Two machines with different values would each push their own on save, and the last-writer-wins merge made them oscillate — an actual write loop, because applying a synced change triggers a save, which triggers a push.

We first tried a convention: keys under a `[local]` table are not synced. That failed because `terminal.fontSize` genuinely belongs next to the other terminal settings, and moving it broke every existing config and every doc link.

## Fix

`crates/sync/src/policy.rs` holds an explicit `NON_SYNCED: &[&str]` list of dotted paths, checked at diff time in both directions. Additionally, applying a remote change now sets a thread-local `applying_remote` guard so the resulting save does not re-enter the push path — that guard, not the denylist, is what actually stopped the oscillation; the denylist stopped the values from being wrong.

Adding a new machine-local setting requires adding it to that list, so the list has a test asserting every key in it exists in the schema.

pages.title: Telemetry events are batched to a 60s flush with a 50-event cap, and dropped rather than persisted on failure
pages.body:
## Почему не отправляем сразу

Первая версия слала HTTP-запрос на каждое событие. На активной сессии это давало 20-40 запросов в минуту, и — что важнее — каждый запрос был отдельным TLS-хендшейком с корпоративного ноутбука, из-за чего у части пользователей срабатывали DLP-правила и соединения резались. Плюс на metered-соединениях это заметный трафик.

Сейчас события копятся в кольцевом буфере в памяти. Flush происходит по первому из: 60 секунд, 50 событий, или переход приложения в background. Батч — один gzip-ed JSON POST, обычно 2-6 KB.

## Что происходит при ошибке

Батч **не** сохраняется на диск и не ретраится. Он просто теряется. Это осознанное решение, а не недоделка:

- очередь на диске — это персистентные данные о пользователе, лежащие в файле, который никто не ожидает; это ровно то, чего мы пытались избежать в [[platform-telemetry-opt-in-only]];
- ретраи после долгого офлайна дают всплеск событий с устаревшими таймстемпами, которые ломают любую агрегацию по времени;
- телеметрия у нас и так directional-only при 4% выборке, потеря части батчей не меняет выводов.

## Единственное исключение

Событие `app.crashed` пишется синхронно в `~/.local/state/zenith/pending-crash` перед завершением процесса и отправляется при следующем старте, потому что по определению его нельзя отправить из падающего процесса. Оно подчиняется отдельному согласию на crash-репорты.
